Java · array · access · L2
Concept: List<Integer>.remove(int) removes by index, remove(Object) by value
Misconception: list.remove(x) removes the value x from a List<Integer>.
Explanation: List has two remove overloads. When the argument is an int, Java picks remove(int index) without boxing, so list.remove(1) removes the element at index 1. To remove the value 1, pass an Integer: list.remove(Integer.valueOf(1)), which removes its first occurrence and returns a boolean. removeIf avoids the question entirely when removing every match.
Incorrect:
List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of(5, 1, 7));
list.remove(1); // removes index 1 (the value 1 by coincidence here)
list.remove(5); // IndexOutOfBoundsException: there is no index 5
Correct:
List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of(5, 1, 7));
list.remove(Integer.valueOf(5)); // removes the value 5: [1, 7]
list.removeIf(v -> v == 7);      // removes every 7: [1]
Complexity: O(n) for either overload, because later elements shift left

Java · array · equality · L1
Concept: Compare boxed integers with equals or as ints, never with ==
Misconception: Two Integer values that print the same are == to each other.
Explanation: Integer is an object, and == compares object references. Java caches Integer objects from -128 to 127, so small values often appear to work with ==, then fail for larger values such as 128. Compare with equals, with Integer.compare, or by unboxing to int first. This matters whenever values come out of a List<Integer>, a Map<Integer, Integer> or an Integer[] array.
Incorrect:
List<Integer> a = List.of(1000), b = List.of(1000);
boolean same = a.get(0) == b.get(0); // false: two different Integer objects
Correct:
List<Integer> a = List.of(1000), b = List.of(1000);
boolean same = a.get(0).equals(b.get(0));     // true
boolean alsoSame = a.get(0).intValue() == b.get(0); // true: one side unboxed
Complexity: O(1)

payload.explanation: Java int values wrap around past 2,147,483,647 without any error. (lo + hi) / 2 becomes negative when lo + hi is too large, which breaks binary search on huge arrays, and running sums of large values come out wrong. Compute the midpoint as lo + (hi - lo) / 2, store sums and products in long, and compare with Integer.compare instead of subtracting. JavaScript solutions do not hit this because their numbers are doubles.

Java · array · creation · L1
Concept: Arrays.asList wraps an object array without copying, and cannot grow
Misconception: Arrays.asList creates an ordinary ArrayList that can be resized.
Explanation: Arrays.asList returns a fixed-size List backed by the original array: set writes through to the array, but add and remove throw UnsupportedOperationException. Passing an int[] produces a List<int[]> with one element, because generics cannot hold primitives. For a resizable list, copy into new ArrayList<>(...); for an int[], box it with a stream.
Incorrect:
List<Integer> xs = Arrays.asList(1, 2, 3);
xs.add(4);                                // UnsupportedOperationException
List<int[]> wrapped = Arrays.asList(new int[] {1, 2, 3}); // one element, not three
Correct:
List<Integer> xs = new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(1, 2, 3));
xs.add(4);                                // [1, 2, 3, 4]
List<Integer> boxed = Arrays.stream(new int[] {1, 2, 3}).boxed().collect(Collectors.toList());
Complexity: O(1) for the view, O(n) for a copy

metadata.concept: >> copies the sign bit; >>> shifts in zeros

payload.concept: >> copies the sign bit; >>> shifts in zeros
payload.example_bad:
int steps = 0;
while (n != 0) { n >>= 1; steps++; } // never ends when n is negative
payload.explanation: Java's int is signed two's complement. The arithmetic shift >> fills the vacated top bits with copies of the sign bit, so a negative value stays negative and converges to -1, not 0. The logical shift >>> fills them with zeros, treating the value as unsigned. Use >>> whenever the bits are data rather than a signed number, such as in Reverse Bits or when walking the bits of a value until it becomes 0. Shift distances are taken modulo 32 for int and 64 for long, so use 1L << i for positions above 30.
payload.misconception: Right-shifting any int eventually reaches 0.

metadata.concept: Count or visit set bits with while (n != 0) and n &= n - 1

payload.concept: Count or visit set bits with while (n != 0) and n &= n - 1
payload.example_bad:
int count = 0;
while (n > 0) { n &= n - 1; count++; } // 0 for any n with bit 31 set
payload.explanation: When bit 31 is set, an int is negative, so while (n > 0) never runs and reports zero set bits. LeetCode's Number of 1 Bits passes such values as negative ints. Loop while n != 0 instead. n &= n - 1 clears the lowest set bit, so the loop runs once per set bit and works for any sign. Integer.bitCount(n) gives the same count with a single fast instruction.
payload.misconception: A loop over the set bits of n can use while (n > 0).

metadata.concept: x & -x isolates the lowest set bit; x & (x - 1) clears it

payload.complexity: O(1) per expression; O(set bits) to visit them all
payload.concept: x & -x isolates the lowest set bit; x & (x - 1) clears it
payload.example_bad:
int low = 1;
while ((x & low) == 0) low <<= 1; // loops forever when x == 0
payload.explanation: In two's complement, -x equals ~x + 1: every bit above the lowest set bit of x flips, and that bit and the zeros below it stay the same. So x & -x keeps only the lowest set bit. Subtracting 1 flips the lowest set bit and every zero below it, so x & (x - 1) clears that bit. These two expressions drive set-bit iteration, power-of-two checks and Fenwick trees, whose blocks have length i & -i. Both give 0 when x is 0, so loops must stop there.
payload.misconception: Finding the lowest set bit requires a loop over every position.

metadata.concept: XOR removes values that appear in pairs, leaving the unpaired one

payload.concept: XOR removes values that appear in pairs, leaving the unpaired one
payload.example_bad:
Set<Integer> seen = new HashSet<>();
for (int v : nums) if (!seen.add(v)) seen.remove(v); // works, but O(n) extra space
payload.explanation: XOR is associative and commutative, x ^ x is 0, and x ^ 0 is x. XOR-ing every value in an array therefore cancels every value that appears twice, in any order, and leaves the one that appears once, in O(n) time and O(1) space. Missing Number uses the same idea by XOR-ing every index 0..n with every value: the indices and values pair up except for the missing number.
payload.misconception: Finding the single unpaired value needs a HashSet or a count map.

Java · Java Bits and Bit Manipulation · Overview
This blueprint treats Java's `int` and `long` as fixed-width containers of 32 and 64 bits, taught through the same 14 lenses. Two Java facts shape everything: integers are signed two's complement, so the top bit is the sign and `>>` copies it while `>>>` does not; and shift distances are masked to the type's width, so `1 << 32` is 1. With those in place, the bit idioms behind the Blind 75 bit problems, bitmask sets and Fenwick trees become short and reliable. All code targets Java 17, and ready-to-ingest chunks are in section 10.

metadata.concept: Override equals(Object) and hashCode together, over the same fields

payload.concept: Override equals(Object) and hashCode together, over the same fields
payload.explanation: HashMap and HashSet first use hashCode to pick a bucket, then equals to compare within it. If two objects are equal but return different hash codes, they land in different buckets and are never compared, so the set keeps duplicates and lookups miss. Override equals(Object), not equals(MyType), mark it @Override, and compute hashCode from exactly the fields equals uses. Records generate both correctly.
payload.misconception: Overriding equals is enough for a class to work as a HashMap key or HashSet element.

metadata.concept: Use a record, not an int[], as a composite key

payload.concept: Use a record, not an int[], as a composite key
payload.explanation: Arrays inherit identity-based equals and hashCode, so a new int[] {2, 3} never matches an earlier one with the same contents. A record such as record Cell(int r, int c) generates value-based equals, hashCode and toString from its components, which makes it a correct key in one line. The JavaScript equivalent is a string key like `${r},${c}`. For very large grids, an encoded number (r * cols + c) avoids allocating an object per cell.
payload.misconception: new int[] {r, c} works as a HashSet element or HashMap key for a grid cell.

metadata.concept: A key whose hash changes after insertion is lost inside the map

payload.complexity: O(1) average for get and put
payload.concept: A key whose hash changes after insertion is lost inside the map
payload.explanation: HashMap stores each entry in the bucket chosen by the key's hashCode at insertion time. If a field used by hashCode changes later, the map still holds the entry in the old bucket, but lookups compute the new hash and search elsewhere, so get returns null and containsKey returns false while the entry remains in the map. Use immutable keys: records, String, boxed numbers, or classes with final fields.
payload.misconception: Changing a field of an object already used as a HashMap key updates the key in place.

document:
Java · object · ordering · L3
Concept: Build comparators with factories; never subtract
Misconception: (a, b) -> a.priority() - b.priority() is a safe comparator.
Explanation: Subtraction overflows when the values are far apart, flipping the sign and silently corrupting sorts, TreeSets and PriorityQueues. Comparator.comparingInt, comparingLong and comparing build correct comparators, thenComparing breaks ties, and reversed flips the order. In sorted sets and maps, a comparator that returns 0 treats two objects as the same element, so always break ties down to a unique field when every element must be kept.
Incorrect:
PriorityQueue<Task> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> a.priority() - b.priority());
Correct:
record Task(int priority, long seq, String name) {}
PriorityQueue<Task> pq = new PriorityQueue<>(
  Comparator.comparingInt(Task::priority).thenComparingLong(Task::seq));
Complexity: O(1) per comparison

Java · Java Classes, Records and Object Equality · Equality and hashing track
Java collection implementations use different identity rules. HashMap and HashSet use equals and hashCode; TreeMap and TreeSet determine key or element equivalence through their ordering comparison. A comparison result of zero can therefore merge distinct objects when the comparator is inconsistent with equals. Lists do not require hashing or ordering merely to store objects. Most Java object bugs are a wrong answer to one of them, and they show up as "the set has duplicates" or "the map cannot find my key". Each row is one lesson.

Java · collections · mutation · L1
Concept: Know whether a method returns a view, an unmodifiable wrapper or an independent copy
Misconception: Collections.unmodifiableList, subList and keySet all return safe, independent snapshots.
Explanation: Many collection methods return views backed by their source: subList, keySet, values, entrySet and Arrays.asList. Changes through a view reach the source, and structural changes to the source can invalidate a view. Collections.unmodifiableList is a read-only view: it cannot be changed directly but still shows changes to its source. List.copyOf, Set.copyOf and Map.copyOf create independent immutable copies, and new ArrayList<>(source) creates an independent mutable copy.
Incorrect:
List<Integer> readOnly = Collections.unmodifiableList(source);
source.add(4); // readOnly now shows the 4: it was never a snapshot
Correct:
static List<Integer> snapshot(List<Integer> source) {
  return List.copyOf(source); // independent and immutable; rejects null elements
}
Complexity: O(1) for views and wrappers, O(n) for copies

metadata.concept: Do not change a collection's structure while iterating over it

payload.concept: Do not change a collection's structure while iterating over it
payload.example_bad: for (Integer x : list) if (x < 0) list.remove(x); // ConcurrentModificationException
payload.explanation: The iterators of ArrayList, HashMap, HashSet and the other standard collections are fail-fast: if the collection is structurally modified other than through the iterator, the next step usually throws ConcurrentModificationException. Detection is best-effort, so the absence of an exception proves nothing. Remove with removeIf, with Iterator.remove, or with map.entrySet().removeIf; collect additions and apply them after the loop.
payload.misconception: Removing elements inside a for-each loop works as long as the removed element was already visited.

metadata.concept: Each collection has its own null rule; check it before storing null

payload.concept: Each collection has its own null rule; check it before storing null
payload.example_bad:
Deque<TreeNode> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
queue.offer(node.left); // NullPointerException when left is null
payload.explanation: ArrayList, LinkedList, HashSet and HashMap accept null (HashMap allows one null key and any number of null values). ArrayDeque and PriorityQueue reject null, because their poll and peek return null to mean "empty". TreeSet and TreeMap reject null keys under natural ordering, ConcurrentHashMap rejects null keys and values, and List.of, Set.of, Map.of and the copyOf methods reject null entirely. Avoid storing null in collections; use sentinels or Optional return values instead.
payload.misconception: Every Java collection accepts null elements, keys and values.

payload.concept: One new list per node, and both directions for undirected edges
payload.example_bad:
List<List<Integer>> adj = new ArrayList<>(Collections.nCopies(n, new ArrayList<>()));
for (int[] e : edges) adj.get(e[0]).add(e[1]); // shared list, one direction
payload.explanation: nCopies and Arrays.fill store the same list object n times, so every node ends up with every neighbour. A generic array (new ArrayList[n]) starts with null slots. Create one list per node in a loop. In an undirected graph, edge [u, v] must be added to both u's and v's lists, or traversals cannot move from v back to u and component counts come out too high.
payload.misconception: Collections.nCopies(n, new ArrayList<>()) creates n empty neighbour lists, and each edge only needs to be stored once.

metadata.concept: Track nodes on the current path, not just visited nodes

payload.concept: Track nodes on the current path, not just visited nodes
payload.explanation: Two paths can reach the same node in a directed acyclic graph, as in a diamond. Reaching a node that is already finished is harmless; only reaching a node still on the current path means a cycle. Keep an int[] state with 0 for unvisited, 1 for on the current path and 2 for finished, and start a DFS from every unvisited node. For graphs with very long paths, convert the recursion to an explicit ArrayDeque.
payload.misconception: In a directed graph, reaching an already-visited node during DFS means there is a cycle.

metadata.concept: Merge roots, not nodes; a failed union means the edge closes a cycle

payload.complexity: Nearly O(1) amortised per operation, O(n) space
payload.concept: Merge roots, not nodes; a failed union means the edge closes a cycle
payload.example_bad: void union(int a, int b) { parent[a] = b; } // links nodes, not roots
payload.explanation: Union-find keeps each group as a tree identified by its root, stored in an int[] parent. Merging must link the roots found by find, or unrelated groups get mixed up. Path halving in find and attaching the smaller tree under the larger keep operations nearly O(1). union returning false means both nodes were already connected, so the new edge closes a cycle; decrementing a counter only on successful unions gives the number of groups.
payload.misconception: Merging two groups means setting parent[a] = b.

metadata.concept: Map each original Node to its copy, and create each copy exactly once

payload.concept: Map each original Node to its copy, and create each copy exactly once
payload.explanation: Graphs have cycles, so naive recursive copying never ends, and shared neighbours get copied several times. Keep a HashMap<Node, Node> from each original to its copy. Clone Graph's Node class does not override equals or hashCode, so the map compares nodes by identity, which is exactly right here. Create a copy the first time a node is seen, then wire each copied node's neighbour list from the map.
payload.misconception: A graph can be deep-copied by recursively copying each node's neighbours.

Teach Java graphs through the same 14 lenses as the JavaScript blueprint, with the same two emphases: most graph bugs happen while building the adjacency list, and most graph problems are solved by recognising which standard algorithm the question asks for (the JavaScript blueprint's decision diagram applies unchanged). All code targets Java 17, and ready-to-ingest chunks are in section 10.

metadata.concept: Compare char board cells with char literals such as '1', never with 1

payload.concept: Compare char board cells with char literals such as '1', never with 1
payload.example_bad:
if (grid[r][c] == 1) count++; // never true on a char[][] board
grid[r][c] = 0;               // stores '\u0000', not '0'
payload.explanation: LeetCode passes many boards as char[][], so each cell holds a character such as '1' or '0'. A char is a number holding a character code: '1' is 49. grid[r][c] == 1 compiles, because char is promoted to int, and is always false. Assigning grid[r][c] = 0 stores the character with code 0, not '0'. Compare and assign with char literals, and convert a digit cell to its value with grid[r][c] - '0'.
payload.misconception: A char[][] cell that displays as 1 can be compared with the number 1.

metadata.concept: grid.clone() copies the row references, not the rows

payload.concept: grid.clone() copies the row references, not the rows
payload.example_bad:
int[][] copy = grid.clone();
copy[0][0] = 9; // grid[0][0] is now 9 as well
payload.explanation: A Java 2D array is an array of row arrays. clone() copies only the outer array, so the copy holds references to the same rows, and writing copy[0][0] also changes grid[0][0]. payload.concept: Flood fill with an explicit ArrayDeque to avoid StackOverflowError
payload.explanation: A recursive flood fill uses one stack frame per cell on its current path, and a large snake-shaped or solid region can make that path hundreds of thousands of cells long, which throws StackOverflowError. An explicit ArrayDeque of cells has no such limit. Mark cells when pushing them (in a boolean[][] or by overwriting the board), so no cell is pushed twice.

Java · heap · creation · L1
Concept: PriorityQueue is a min-heap by default; reverse it for max, and never subtract in comparators
Misconception: new PriorityQueue<>() returns the largest element first, and (a, b) -> b - a is a safe max-heap comparator.
Explanation: PriorityQueue orders by natural order or the given comparator and returns the smallest element first. For a max-heap pass Comparator.reverseOrder(). Comparators built by subtraction overflow when values are far apart, which silently misorders the heap; use Integer.compare, Comparator.comparingInt or comparingLong. Types that are not Comparable, including int[], need a comparator or the first offer throws ClassCastException.
Incorrect:
PriorityQueue<Integer> maxHeap = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> b - a); // overflows on extremes
PriorityQueue<int[]> pairs = new PriorityQueue<>();                    // ClassCastException on offer
Correct:
PriorityQueue<Integer> maxHeap = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.reverseOrder());
PriorityQueue<int[]> pairs = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]));
Complexity: O(log n) per offer and poll

payload.explanation: PriorityQueue stores a binary heap in an array, and toString and iterators walk that array. PriorityQueue<Integer> heap = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.reverseOrder());
for (int x : nums) { heap.offer(x); if (heap.size() > k) heap.poll(); } // keeps the k smallest
payload.explanation: A size-k heap must make it cheap to evict the weakest of the k items kept. For the k largest, the weakest is the smallest, which a min-heap keeps at its head: offer each value and poll when the size exceeds k. The head is then the k-th largest. The same reasoning gives a max-heap for the k smallest or the k closest. This takes O(n log k) time and O(k) memory, and also works on streams.
payload.misconception: The k largest values belong in a max-heap.

metadata.concept: Re-offer instead of editing an element's priority in place

payload.complexity: O(log n) per new entry; stale entries cost one extra poll each
payload.concept: Re-offer instead of editing an element's priority in place
payload.example_bad: task.priority = 0; // task is already in the heap; it will not move to the front
payload.explanation: The heap positions an element only when it is offered or when neighbouring elements move. Changing a field the comparator reads leaves the element where it was, so later polls return elements out of order without any error. PriorityQueue has no decrease-key: either remove the element (O(n)), change it and offer it again, or offer a new entry and skip stale ones when they are polled, as Dijkstra does. When priorities change often, a TreeMap or TreeSet with a tie-breaker supports O(log n) updates.
payload.misconception: Updating a field of an object inside a PriorityQueue updates its position.

Java · Java Heaps and Priority Queues · Overview
Teach Java heaps through the same 14 lenses as the JavaScript blueprint. The difference that shapes everything: Java ships `PriorityQueue`, a binary min-heap, so the curriculum moves from building a heap to using one correctly. That means choosing min or max, writing comparators that never subtract, knowing that iteration and printing are not sorted, and never changing an element's priority after inserting it. A compact hand-built `int` heap remains for interviews that ask for one. All code targets Java 17, and ready-to-ingest chunks are in section 10.

metadata.concept: A dummy node before the head removes every special case for the head

payload.concept: A dummy node before the head removes every special case for the head
payload.explanation: Removing a node means changing the next field of the node before it, and the head has no node before it, so code without a dummy needs an extra branch and often throws NullPointerException on prev.next. Creating new ListNode(0, head) gives every real node a predecessor. Build or edit behind the dummy, then return dummy.next, which is the new head even if the original head was removed.
payload.misconception: Functions that may remove or replace the head need separate code for the head.

metadata.concept: Reverse with three pointers, saving next before rewiring

payload.complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space iteratively; O(n) stack recursively
payload.concept: Reverse with three pointers, saving next before rewiring
payload.explanation: The iterative reversal keeps prev, cur and next. Saving cur.next before overwriting it is essential: once cur.next points backwards, the rest of the list is unreachable. The recursive version uses one stack frame per node, and Java performs no tail-call optimisation, so it throws StackOverflowError on lists of tens of thousands of nodes. Use the iterative version by default.
payload.misconception: A recursive reversal is as safe as an iterative one.

metadata.concept: Loop while fast != null && fast.next != null

payload.concept: Loop while fast != null && fast.next != null
payload.example_bad: while (fast.next != null) { slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next; }
payload.explanation: fast moves two nodes per step, so on even-length lists it can land on null itself, and reading fast.next then throws NullPointerException. Check fast first, then fast.next. With both pointers starting at head, the loop stops with slow at the middle (the second of two middles on even lengths). For cycle detection, compare slow == fast by reference, never by value.
payload.misconception: Checking fast.next != null is enough before moving fast two steps.

metadata.concept: LinkedList.get(i) walks the list, so index loops are O(n^2)

payload.complexity: O(n) with iteration, O(n^2) with get(i) in a loop
payload.concept: LinkedList.get(i) walks the list, so index loops are O(n^2)
payload.example_bad:
long sum = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < list.size(); i++) sum += list.get(i); // O(n^2) on a LinkedList
payload.explanation: LinkedList implements List, but its nodes are not indexed: get(i) walks from the nearer end, O(n) per call, so a for loop with get(i) is O(n^2). Iterate with an enhanced for or a ListIterator, whose remove and add are O(1) at the cursor. For index access use ArrayList; for queues and stacks use ArrayDeque. LinkedList also has the remove(int) overload, which removes by index on a LinkedList<Integer>.
payload.misconception: java.util.LinkedList is a List, so get(i) is as cheap as on an ArrayList.

Java · language · mental-model · L0
Concept: int is 32 bits, long is 64, and both wrap silently on overflow
Misconception: Java numbers behave like JavaScript numbers and never lose precision for whole values.
Explanation: Java's int holds values from -2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647 and long from about -9.2e18 to 9.2e18. Arithmetic that leaves the range wraps around without an error. char is a 16-bit unsigned number, and byte and short are promoted to int in expressions. Use long for sums, products and anything that can exceed about two billion.
Incorrect:
int big = 2_000_000_000 + 2_000_000_000; // -294967296
Correct:
long big = 2_000_000_000L + 2_000_000_000L; // 4000000000
Complexity: O(1)

Java · language · equality · L0
Concept: Collections hold Integer objects; unboxing null throws, and == compares references
Misconception: int and Integer are interchangeable everywhere.
Explanation: Generic collections cannot hold primitives, so Java boxes int values into Integer objects and unboxes them automatically. Unboxing null, for example a missing map value, throws NullPointerException. Integer objects compared with == are compared by reference, which works for cached values from -128 to 127 and fails above. Compare with equals, or unbox first.
Incorrect:
Integer a = 1000, b = 1000;
boolean same = a == b; // false
Correct:
Integer a = 1000, b = 1000;
boolean same = a.equals(b); // true
Complexity: O(1), plus an allocation per boxed value outside the cache

Java · array · mental-model · L0
Concept: Arrays have a fixed length, a single element type and default values
Misconception: A Java array grows when you write past its end.
Explanation: new int[n] creates n zeros; new String[n] creates n nulls. The length is fixed and read with the length field (no parentheses). Any index outside 0..length - 1 throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. For a growing sequence, use ArrayList.
Incorrect:
int[] a = new int[3];
a[3] = 1; // ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
Correct:
int[] a = new int[3];
for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) a[i] = i * i; // [0, 1, 4]
Complexity: O(1) access, O(n) to create

Java · array · creation · L0
Concept: ArrayList grows on add; its constructor argument is capacity, not size
Misconception: new ArrayList<>(n) creates a list of n elements.
Explanation: ArrayList is a resizable array of references. add appends in amortised O(1); get and set are O(1); adding or removing in the middle is O(n). The int passed to the constructor only reserves capacity: the list is still empty, so set(0, x) throws. size() reports the number of elements.
Incorrect:
List<Integer> xs = new ArrayList<>(3);
xs.set(0, 5); // IndexOutOfBoundsException: size is 0
Correct:
List<Integer> xs = new ArrayList<>();
xs.add(5);
int first = xs.get(0); // 5
Complexity: O(1) get and amortised add at the end

Java · string · mutation · L0
Concept: Strings are immutable; every method returns a new string
Misconception: Calling s.toUpperCase() or s.trim() changes s.
Explanation: A Java String never changes after creation. Methods such as toUpperCase, replace, trim and substring return new strings, so their results must be assigned. length() counts UTF-16 code units, charAt(i) returns a char, and out-of-range positions throw StringIndexOutOfBoundsException.
Incorrect:
s.toUpperCase(); // the result is discarded; s is unchanged
Correct:
s = s.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT);
Complexity: O(n) for methods that build a new string

Java · collections · creation · L0
Concept: Collections are interfaces with implementations, and they hold objects, not primitives
Misconception: List<int> declares a list of ints.
Explanation: Generic types take reference types only, so a list of numbers is List<Integer>, with automatic boxing. Each collection interface has a default implementation: ArrayList for List, HashSet for Set, HashMap for Map, and ArrayDeque for stacks, queues and deques. Concept: Remove from a list with removeIf or an Iterator, never inside a for-each loop
Misconception: Removing elements inside a for-each loop over the same list is safe.
Explanation: An enhanced for loop uses the list's iterator, and removing through the list changes it under that iterator, which usually throws ConcurrentModificationException. Concept: Comparators must not subtract ints
Misconception: (a, b) -> a - b is a correct comparator for any ints.
Explanation: A comparator only needs the sign of its result, and subtraction gives the right sign until it overflows: with Integer.MIN_VALUE and 1, a - b wraps to a large positive number and the order flips. Correct:

  Arrays.sort(boxed, Integer::compare);

Teach Java maps through the same 14 lenses as the JavaScript Map blueprint, with two Java-only emphases: keys match by `equals` and `hashCode`, so key types must match exactly and stay unchanged; and Java offers three map types with different orderings, including `TreeMap`, a sorted map with floor and ceiling queries that JavaScript has no built-in equivalent for. All code targets Java 17, and ready-to-ingest chunks are in section 10.

Java · Java Maps (HashMap, LinkedHashMap, TreeMap) · Key and lookup track
Most Java map bugs happen at the lookup: `get` returns `null` for three different reasons (absent key, a stored `null`, a key of the wrong type), and boxed values bring the `Integer` equality trap with them. Java 8's `merge` and `compute` methods remove most of the hand-written lookup code where these bugs live. Each row is one lesson.

metadata.concept: offer, poll and peek return special values; add, remove and element throw

payload.concept: offer, poll and peek return special values; add, remove and element throw
payload.explanation: Java's Queue interface has two parallel families. offer, poll and peek report failure with false or null; add, remove and element throw (IllegalStateException when a bounded queue is full, NoSuchElementException when the queue is empty). Pick one family per codebase. With poll and peek, never unbox the result into an int without checking for null first, and never store null in the queue, since ArrayDeque rejects it.
payload.misconception: poll and remove are interchangeable ways to take the head of a queue.

metadata.concept: Read queue.size() once per level, before adding children

payload.concept: Read queue.size() once per level, before adding children
payload.explanation: The loop condition is re-evaluated every iteration, and the queue's size changes as nodes are polled and their children offered, so the loop runs the wrong number of times and mixes levels. Read the size once into a variable before the loop: for (int size = queue.size(); size > 0; size--). Children added during the loop then wait for the next level.
payload.misconception: for (int i = 0; i < queue.size(); i++) processes exactly one level of a BFS.

metadata.concept: ArrayList.remove(0) is O(n); ArrayDeque.poll is O(1)

payload.complexity: O(V + E) with ArrayDeque, O(V^2 + E) with ArrayList.remove(0)
payload.concept: ArrayList.remove(0) is O(n); ArrayDeque.poll is O(1)
payload.explanation: ArrayList stores elements contiguously, so removing index 0 shifts every remaining element left: O(n) per removal and O(n^2) for a BFS over n nodes. This is the Java version of JavaScript's shift problem. ArrayDeque is a circular array whose head simply moves, so offer and poll are O(1) amortised. LinkedList is also O(1) but allocates a node per element and exposes List methods such as remove(int) that are easy to call by mistake.
payload.misconception: Any list works as a BFS queue if items are removed from the front.

metadata.concept: Keep window candidates in a deque of indices with decreasing values

payload.concept: Keep window candidates in a deque of indices with decreasing values
payload.explanation: An element can never be a window's maximum once a larger element appears after it, so it can be discarded from the back. An element also stops mattering once its index leaves the window, so it is discarded from the front. A Deque<Integer> of indices with values decreasing from front to back keeps the current maximum at the front. Each index is offered once and polled at most once, so the whole pass is O(n).
payload.misconception: The maximum of each sliding window has to be found by scanning the window.

metadata.concept: Fenwick trees are 1-indexed; updates climb with i += i & -i and queries descend with i -= i & -i

payload.complexity: O(log n) per add and prefix
payload.concept: Fenwick trees are 1-indexed; updates climb with i += i & -i and queries descend with i -= i & -i
payload.explanation: Each tree[i] stores the sum of the block (i - lowbit(i), i], where lowbit(i) = i & -i. At i = 0 the lowbit is 0, so a loop starting there never advances and the program hangs. Store the tree 1-indexed in a long[n + 1] and add 1 to caller indices at the boundary. Updates climb to every block that contains i; prefix queries descend through disjoint blocks that together cover [1, i]. Set operations must add the difference from the current value.
payload.misconception: A Fenwick tree can be indexed from 0 like any other array.

metadata.concept: Start every query at the operation's identity, and use one range convention per class

payload.concept: Start every query at the operation's identity, and use one range convention per class
payload.explanation: A segment tree combines node values with an associative operation, so each query starts from that operation's identity: 0 for sums, Long.MAX_VALUE for minimums, Long.MIN_VALUE for maximums. Starting a minimum at 0 returns 0 for any all-positive range. The compact iterative tree queries the half-open range [l, r); mixing it with inclusive callers drops or adds an element, so document the convention and convert once at the boundary.
payload.misconception: A query accumulator can always start at 0.

metadata.concept: Turn large or negative values into small ranks before indexing a tree by value

payload.concept: Turn large or negative values into small ranks before indexing a tree by value
payload.example_bad: Fenwick f = new Fenwick(1_000_000_001); // one slot per possible value, and negatives fail
payload.explanation: When a tree is indexed by value (to count smaller elements, inversions or order statistics), values may be huge or negative. Sort the distinct values; each value's rank is its index in that sorted array, found with Arrays.binarySearch or a HashMap. The tree then needs only as many slots as there are distinct values. Ranks must come from a sorted, deduplicated array, or binary search returns wrong or negative positions.
payload.misconception: A Fenwick tree indexed by value needs an array as large as the largest value.

Java · Java Segment Trees and Fenwick Trees · From prefix sums to Fenwick trees
Prefix sums answer any range sum in O(1), but one update to `a[i]` changes every prefix after `i`: O(n). A Fenwick tree splits the difference, giving O(log n) for both. Its whole implementation is two loops over one idea: `i & -i`, the lowest set bit of `i`, which is the length of the block `tree[i]` covers.

Java · Java Segment Trees and Fenwick Trees · Segment tree track
A segment tree stores, for every node, the answer for a range of the array: the root covers everything, each child covers half its parent, and the leaves are single elements. Any query range is covered exactly by O(log n) nodes, and an update changes one leaf and its O(log n) ancestors.

[Diagram: segment tree · 8 leaves, query [2, 5]]

The query never visits the leaves 2 to 5: two internal nodes already hold their combined sum.

Java · set · equality · L3
Concept: TreeSet treats elements the comparator calls equal as duplicates
Misconception: A TreeSet keeps every distinct element and only uses the comparator for ordering.
Explanation: TreeSet does not call equals. Two elements are the same element if the comparator returns 0 for them, so a comparator that compares only part of an element silently drops others with the same key. Sorting strings by length keeps only one string of each length. Break ties with further comparisons until 0 means the elements are truly equal.
Incorrect:
TreeSet<String> byLength = new TreeSet<>(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length));
byLength.addAll(List.of("ab", "cd", "e")); // [e, ab]: "cd" was dropped
Correct:
TreeSet<String> byLength = new TreeSet<>(
  Comparator.comparingInt(String::length).thenComparing(Comparator.naturalOrder()));
byLength.addAll(List.of("ab", "cd", "e")); // [e, ab, cd]
Complexity: O(log n) per operation

Java · set · edge-cases · L4
Concept: int shifts use only the low 5 bits of the distance; use long for more than 31 bits
Misconception: 1 << 40 sets bit 40 of a mask.
Explanation: For an int, Java masks the shift distance to its low 5 bits, so 1 << 32 is 1 and 1 << 40 is 256. Bit 31 is also the sign bit, so 1 << 31 is negative. For masks wider than 31 bits, use a long and write 1L << i, which allows bits 0 to 63. Test bits with parentheses, (mask & (1 << i)) != 0, because != binds more tightly than &.
Incorrect:
long mask = 0;
mask |= 1 << 40;                 // sets bit 8, not bit 40
boolean on = (mask & 1 << 40) != 0;
Correct:
long mask = 0;
mask |= 1L << 40;                // bit 40
boolean on = (mask & (1L << 40)) != 0;
int count = Long.bitCount(mask); // 1
Complexity: O(1)

metadata.concept: Declare stacks as Deque and implement them with ArrayDeque

payload.concept: Declare stacks as Deque and implement them with ArrayDeque
payload.explanation: Stack is a legacy class that extends Vector: every method is synchronized, it exposes index access such as get(0), and it iterates from bottom to top. The Java documentation recommends the Deque interface instead. ArrayDeque is faster, its push, pop and peek all work at the head, and it iterates from top to bottom. It rejects null elements.
payload.misconception: java.util.Stack is the standard Java stack.

document:
Java · stack · mutation · L1
Concept: pop throws on an empty stack; peek and poll return null
Misconception: Popping or peeking an empty Java stack returns a harmless default, as in JavaScript.
Explanation: ArrayDeque.pop throws NoSuchElementException on an empty stack (Stack.pop throws EmptyStackException). peek and poll return null instead, and assigning that null to an int throws NullPointerException during unboxing. Guard every pop and every peek into a primitive with isEmpty(), especially in monotonic-stack while loops.
Incorrect:
while (stack.peek() < nums[i]) stack.pop(); // NullPointerException once the stack empties
Correct:
static void popSmaller(Deque<Integer> stack, int value) {

payload.explanation: ArrayDeque.pop throws NoSuchElementException on an empty stack (Stack.pop throws EmptyStackException). peek and poll return null instead, and assigning that null to an int throws NullPointerException during unboxing. Guard every pop and every peek into a primitive with isEmpty(), especially in monotonic-stack while loops.

metadata.concept: ArrayDeque iterates from the top; Stack iterates from the bottom

payload.concept: ArrayDeque iterates from the top; Stack iterates from the bottom
payload.explanation: ArrayDeque used as a stack keeps the top at its head, so iteration, printing and copying into a list all go from top to bottom. The legacy Stack keeps the top at the end of its Vector, so it goes from bottom to top. Mixing add or offer into an ArrayDeque stack puts items at the tail, which is the bottom, silently breaking last-in-first-out order.
payload.misconception: Every Java stack prints and iterates in the order items were pushed.

metadata.concept: Deep recursion throws StackOverflowError; an explicit ArrayDeque removes the limit

payload.complexity: O(n) time, O(n) heap space instead of call-stack space
payload.concept: Deep recursion throws StackOverflowError; an explicit ArrayDeque removes the limit
payload.explanation: Each recursive call uses a frame on the thread's stack, which is limited, and Java performs no tail-call optimisation. A skewed tree or a long path of tens of thousands of nodes throws StackOverflowError, an Error that should not be caught. Pushing pending work onto an ArrayDeque gives the same traversal with no depth limit. Running recursion on a thread with a larger requested stack is a workaround only, because the size is a hint the JVM may ignore.
payload.misconception: A recursive solution that passes small tests works for any input size.

Java · string · equality · L0
Concept: Compare string contents with equals; == compares references
Misconception: == compares the text of two strings, because it works on string literals.
Explanation: String is an object, and == checks whether two references point to the same object. Literals and compile-time constants are interned in the string pool, so "a" == "a" is true, which makes == look correct in small tests. Strings built at runtime (input, concatenation, substring) are separate objects, so == fails on equal text. Use equals for content, call it on the value that cannot be null ("yes".equals(input)), or use Objects.equals when either side may be null.
Incorrect:
String a = "ab";
String b = new StringBuilder("a").append("b").toString();
boolean same = a == b; // false: two different objects with the same text
Correct:
String a = "ab";
String b = new StringBuilder("a").append("b").toString();
boolean same = a.equals(b);                // true
boolean safe = java.util.Objects.equals(a, null); // false, and no NullPointerException
Complexity: O(n) for equals in the worst case

Java · string · access · L1
Concept: A char is a 16-bit number, so char arithmetic produces ints
Misconception: Adding two chars, or a char and a number, produces text.
Explanation: A Java char is an unsigned 16-bit integer holding one UTF-16 code unit. Arithmetic promotes it to int: 'a' + 1 is 98 and 'a' + 'b' is 195. This is useful for indexing, since c - 'a' maps lowercase letters to 0..25, and digit - '0' gives a digit's value. To get a character back, cast: (char) ('a' + 1) is 'b'. Concatenation happens only once a String is involved, evaluated left to right.
Incorrect:
char c = 'a';
System.out.println(c + 1);     // 98
System.out.println('a' + 'b'); // 195
Correct:
char c = 'a';
System.out.println((char) (c + 1));   // b
System.out.println("" + 'a' + 'b');   // ab
int[] count = new int[26];
count[c - 'a']++;                     // index 0
Complexity: O(1)

Java · string · transformation · L1
Concept: String.split treats its argument as a regex and removes trailing empty strings
Misconception: s.split(".") splits on dots, and every field in the input appears in the result.
Explanation: split takes a regular expression, so "." matches every character and "a.b.c".split(".") returns an empty array. Escape metacharacters with "\\." or Pattern.quote("."). split also removes trailing empty strings unless the limit argument is negative, so "a,b,,".split(",") has two elements while split(",", -1) has four. Leading empty strings are kept.
Incorrect:
String[] parts = "a.b.c".split(".");   // length 0
String[] fields = "a,b,,".split(","); // length 2: the empty fields are gone
Correct:
String[] parts = "a.b.c".split(java.util.regex.Pattern.quote(".")); // [a, b, c]
String[] fields = "a,b,,".split(",", -1);                           // [a, b, , ]
Complexity: O(n) per call, plus regex compilation for non-trivial patterns

String[] fields = "a,b,,".split(",", -1);                           // [a, b, , ]
payload.explanation: split takes a regular expression, so "." matches every character and "a.b.c".split(".") returns an empty array. Escape metacharacters with "\\." or Pattern.quote("."). split also removes trailing empty strings unless the limit argument is negative, so "a,b,,".split(",") has two elements while split(",", -1) has four. Leading empty strings are kept.
payload.misconception: s.split(".") splits on dots, and every field in the input appears in the result.

payload.complexity: O(n) with StringBuilder vs O(n^2) with +=

payload.example_bad:
String result = "";
for (char c : s.toCharArray()) if (Character.isLetterOrDigit(c)) result += Character.toLowerCase(c);
payload.explanation: Strings are immutable, so result += c creates a new String and copies every character built so far. Over n iterations that is O(n^2) work. A StringBuilder appends into one growing buffer in amortised O(1) per character; call toString() once at the end. Its equals method compares references, so compare builders through toString() or compareTo.
payload.misconception: result += c inside a loop is as cheap as appending to a list.

Java · Java Strings · Unicode track
Java strings use the same three levels as JavaScript ones: UTF-16 code units (what `char`, `charAt` and `length()` see), code points (what `codePoints()` sees) and graphemes (what a person sees). Most interview problems promise lowercase English letters, so `char`-based techniques are correct there, but learners should know exactly where they stop being correct.

```java
String s = "e\u0301\uD83D\uDC4D\uD83C\uDFFD"; // e + combining accent, thumbs up + skin tone
s.length();                                  // 6 UTF-16 code units
s.codePointCount(0, s.length());             // 4 code points
Normalizer.normalize(s, Normalizer.Form.NFC).length(); // 5: e + accent becomes one code point
new StringBuilder(s).reverse();              // keeps each surrogate pair together
```

metadata.concept: Pass long bounds down a BST check so extreme int values stay valid

payload.concept: Pass long bounds down a BST check so extreme int values stay valid
payload.explanation: The BST rule must hold for whole subtrees, so a correct check passes an open interval (low, high) down each path. If the initial bounds are Integer.MIN_VALUE and Integer.MAX_VALUE, a node whose value equals one of them fails the strict comparison, so the single-node tree [2147483647] is wrongly reported invalid. Use long bounds starting at Long.MIN_VALUE and Long.MAX_VALUE, or nullable Integer bounds where null means unbounded.
payload.misconception: Integer.MIN_VALUE and Integer.MAX_VALUE are safe "no bound" values for Validate BST.

metadata.concept: Keep state that must survive recursive calls in a field or return value, not an int parameter

payload.concept: Keep state that must survive recursive calls in a field or return value, not an int parameter
payload.explanation: Java passes primitives by value, so each call gets its own copy of k, and decrementing it changes nothing for the caller or for later calls. JavaScript solutions often hide this by closing over a variable, but Java lambdas and helpers cannot reassign captured locals. Keep the counter in a field (reset in the public method), in a one-element int[], or return the updated count from each call.
payload.misconception: Decrementing an int parameter inside a recursive call is visible to the caller.

metadata.concept: Record new ArrayList<>(path), and remove the last element when backtracking

payload.complexity: O(n · h) time including copies, O(h) for the path
payload.concept: Record new ArrayList<>(path), and remove the last element when backtracking
payload.example_bad: if (node.left == null && node.right == null && remaining == node.val) result.add(path);
payload.explanation: Java passes a copy of the List reference by value. These recursive calls refer to the same mutable path object; rebinding a parameter would not rebind the caller's variable. Adding it to the result stores a reference to that same object, which keeps changing and is usually empty when the search ends. Copy it with new ArrayList<>(path) at the moment it is recorded, and undo each choice after the recursive calls with path.remove(path.size() - 1), where remove(int) removing by index is exactly what is wanted.
payload.misconception: result.add(path) saves the current path.

metadata.concept: Write null markers to the output, but queue only real nodes

payload.concept: Write null markers to the output, but queue only real nodes
payload.example_bad:
queue.offer(node.left);  // NullPointerException when node.left is null
queue.offer(node.right);
payload.explanation: Serialisation must record missing children, or different trees produce the same string. ArrayDeque, the usual Java queue, throws NullPointerException when offered null. Append a marker such as # to the StringBuilder for each missing child and queue only real nodes. When deserialising, handle the empty string first, because "".split(",") returns one empty token, and check for the marker before calling Integer.parseInt.
payload.misconception: Level-order serialisation can queue null children like any other node.

Teach Java binary trees through the same 14 lenses as the JavaScript blueprint, with the recursion contract as the signature skill: what each call returns for `null`, passes down, and returns up. metadata.concept: Node[26] children are fast and alphabetical, but accept only lowercase a-z

payload.complexity: O(1) per step; 26 references per node
payload.concept: Node[26] children are fast and alphabetical, but accept only lowercase a-z
payload.example_bad: node = node.next[word.charAt(i) - 'a']; // throws for 'A', '3' or 'é'; NPE later if the slot is null
payload.explanation: An array of 26 child references indexed by c - 'a' is the idiomatic Java trie for lowercase input: O(1) child lookup, and iterating indices 0 to 25 visits children in alphabetical order. Every other character produces an index outside 0..25 and throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException ('A' - 'a' is -32). New arrays start as 26 nulls, so check before descending. When input is not guaranteed lowercase, normalise it or use Map<Character, Node> children (TreeMap for sorted output).
payload.misconception: A Node[26] trie works for any word, as long as the index is computed with c - 'a'.

metadata.concept: A path is a prefix; only an end marker makes it a word

payload.concept: A path is a prefix; only an end marker makes it a word
payload.explanation: Inserting "car" creates nodes for "c", "ca" and "car", and only the last gets end = true. search must walk the path and check end; startsWith only needs the walk to succeed. With only "car" stored, search("ca") is false and startsWith("ca") is true. In Java, a shared find method that returns the node or null keeps both operations short.
payload.misconception: If the walk for a string reaches a node, the string is a stored word.

metadata.concept: Reuse one StringBuilder; append before each child and setLength after

payload.complexity: O(nodes visited) plus O(L) per recorded word
payload.concept: Reuse one StringBuilder; append before each child and setLength after
payload.example_bad: collect(node.next[c], path + (char) ('a' + c), out); // a new String at every node
payload.explanation: Strings are immutable, so path + ch copies the whole path at every node visited, which adds O(L) work and an allocation per node. A single StringBuilder can be shared by the whole search: append the character before descending into a child, and call setLength(length - 1) after returning to undo it. Call toString() only when a word is recorded. With Node[26] children, looping c from 0 to 25 returns words alphabetically.
payload.misconception: Passing path + ch to each recursive call is an efficient way to build words in a trie DFS.

metadata.concept: Store words on end nodes, mark char cells with '#', restore them, and prune

payload.complexity: O(m · n · 4 · 3^(L-1)) worst case; pruning removes most of it in practice
payload.concept: Store words on end nodes, mark char cells with '#', restore them, and prune
payload.example_bad: for (String w : words) if (exist(board, w)) found.add(w); // one full board search per word
payload.explanation: Build a trie of the words and store each word on its end node. Run one DFS from every cell that walks the char[][] board and the trie together: mark the cell with '#' before exploring and restore the original char afterwards. Report a word when its node is reached, then set node.word = null so it is reported once. After exploring a node, remove it from its parent if it has no word and no children, so later searches skip finished branches.

Teach Java tries through the same 14 lenses as the JavaScript blueprint: a trie stores shared prefixes once, every operation walks one character per level, and a word exists only where a node is marked as an end. metadata.concept: A group is identified by its root; union and connectivity both work on roots

payload.concept: A group is identified by its root; union and connectivity both work on roots
payload.example_bad:
void union(int a, int b) { parent[a] = b; }
boolean connected(int a, int b) { return parent[a] == parent[b]; }
payload.explanation: Union-find stores each group as a tree in an int[] parent, and only the root (the node that is its own parent) identifies the group. Setting parent[a] = b moves only a, leaving the rest of a's group behind. Two members of one group can have different direct parents, so comparing parent[a] with parent[b] gives false negatives. Always call find on both sides, link one root under the other, and compare roots.
payload.misconception: parent[a] = b merges a's and b's groups, and parent[a] == parent[b] means they are connected.

metadata.concept: Path compression plus union by size make union-find nearly O(1) per operation

payload.concept: Path compression plus union by size make union-find nearly O(1) per operation
payload.example_bad: int find(int x) { return parent[x] == x ? x : find(parent[x]); } // no compression, recursive
payload.explanation: Without optimisations, unions can build a chain, and find walks the whole chain: O(n) per call. Union by size attaches the smaller tree under the larger, which keeps trees shallow. Path compression makes every node visited by find point to the root (or, with halving, to its grandparent), so later finds take one step. Together they give an amortised cost bounded by the inverse Ackermann function, which is at most 4 for any realistic input. Write find iteratively so very large inputs cannot overflow the stack.
payload.misconception: Union-find is fast with or without its optimisations.

metadata.concept: Use a HashMap parent for labels, created on first sight and compared with equals

payload.complexity: Nearly O(1) amortised per operation, plus hashing
payload.concept: Use a HashMap parent for labels, created on first sight and compared with equals
payload.example_bad: if (find(a) == find(b)) return; // compares String references
payload.explanation: When elements are strings (emails, variable names), store parent links in a HashMap<String, String>, adding each element as its own parent the first time it appears. Compare roots with equals, because == compares String references. For many operations, mapping each label to an integer id once and using the array-based class is faster.
payload.misconception: The integer union-find works for strings once they are used as array indices.

metadata.concept: Store each node's ratio to its parent, and combine ratios along the path

payload.concept: Store each node's ratio to its parent, and combine ratios along the path
payload.example_bad:
weight.put(x, weight.get(x) * weight.get(p)); // before find(p): p's weight is not yet relative to the root
parent.put(x, find(p));
payload.explanation: Weighted union-find keeps weight(x) = value(x) / value(parent(x)). During find, after the parent has been compressed, multiply x's weight by its parent's weight so x points straight at the root with the correct ratio. To union a / b = ratio, link a's root under b's root with weight ratio * weight(b) / weight(a). Two variables with the same root answer a / b as weight(a) / weight(b); different roots mean the answer is unknown.
payload.misconception: Ratio questions such as a / c from a / b and b / c need a graph search per query.

Java · Java Union-Find (Disjoint Set) · Core operations track
Union-find is two operations on one array. `find` walks to the root; `union` links two roots. Two optimisations keep the trees shallow: path compression (during `find`, point visited nodes closer to the root) and union by size (attach the smaller tree under the larger).

[Diagram: path compression · 4 elements, one group]

A chain like the one on the left forms when unions always attach the larger tree under the smaller; union by size prevents it, and path compression repairs it on the first `find`.

JavaScript · array · access · L2
Concept: Removing elements while looping
Misconception: A forward loop with splice(i, 1) visits every element.
Explanation: splice shifts every later element left by one, so after removing index i the next element slides into i and the loop's i++ skips it. Loop backwards so the shift only touches elements already visited, or compact with a write pointer in one pass.
Incorrect:
for (let i = 0; i < a.length; i++) if (a[i] === 0) a.splice(i, 1);
Correct:
for (let i = a.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) if (a[i] === 0) a.splice(i, 1);
Complexity: O(n^2) worst case with backwards splice; O(n) with a write pointer

JavaScript · array · ordering · L1
Concept: sort() without a comparator sorts numbers as strings
Misconception: [10, 9, 1].sort() sorts the numbers in ascending order.
Explanation: With no comparator, sort converts every element to a string and compares UTF-16 code units, so [10, 9, 1] becomes [1, 10, 9]. Pass (a, b) => a - b for ascending numbers and (a, b) => b - a for descending. sort changes the array in place and returns it; toSorted (ES2023) returns a sorted copy. Sorting is stable, so a tie-break with || keeps multi-key sorts short.
Incorrect:
const nums = [10, 9, 1];
nums.sort(); // [1, 10, 9]
Correct:
const nums = [10, 9, 1];
nums.sort((a, b) => a - b); // [1, 9, 10]
const intervals = [[2, 6], [1, 3], [1, 2]];
intervals.sort((x, y) => x[0] - y[0] || x[1] - y[1]); // [[1, 2], [1, 3], [2, 6]]
Complexity: O(n log n) comparisons

payload.explanation: Arrays are objects, so ===, includes and indexOf compare references, never contents. Compare two arrays by length and then element by element. Spread and slice copy one level; structuredClone copies nested arrays too.

JavaScript · array · edge-cases · L3
Concept: Numbers are exact only up to 2^53 - 1, and bitwise operators work on 32-bit integers
Misconception: JavaScript numbers never overflow, so any integer arithmetic is exact.
Explanation: Every number is a 64-bit double, so integers are exact only up to Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, 2^53 - 1. A product of two values near 1e9 already exceeds that, and a modulo taken afterwards is silently wrong; use BigInt there. Bitwise operators convert to 32-bit signed integers, so (lo + hi) >> 1 turns negative once the sum passes 2^31 - 1. Use Math.floor((lo + hi) / 2) for large ranges.
Incorrect:
const wrong = (123456789 * 987654321) % 1_000_000_007; // the product is not exact
const mid = (0 + 3_000_000_000) >> 1;                  // -647483648
Correct:
const MOD = 1_000_000_007n;
const prod = (123456789n * 987654321n) % MOD;     // exact, as a BigInt
const mid = Math.floor((0 + 3_000_000_000) / 2);  // 1500000000
const safe = Number.isSafeInteger(2 ** 53);       // false
Complexity: O(1) per operation; BigInt arithmetic is slower than number arithmetic

An array is irreplaceable whenever the meaning lives in position: an index is the answer, neighbours matter, ranges must be contiguous, space must be O(1), or index arithmetic encodes structure. metadata.concept: An undirected edge must be stored in both nodes' neighbour lists

payload.concept: An undirected edge must be stored in both nodes' neighbour lists
payload.example_bad:
const adj = Array(n).fill([]);          // one shared list
for (const [u, v] of edges) adj[u].push(v); // one direction only
payload.explanation: In an undirected graph an edge [u, v] lets a traversal move from u to v and from v to u. If it is stored only in u's list, a traversal starting at v never reaches u, so component counts come out too high and reachability checks fail. Add the edge to both lists. Also create each node's list separately: Array(n).fill([]) shares one list between every node.
payload.misconception: Storing each edge once, as given in the input, is enough for an undirected graph.

metadata.concept: Detect a directed cycle by tracking which nodes are on the current path

payload.concept: Detect a directed cycle by tracking which nodes are on the current path
payload.explanation: In a directed graph two paths can lead to the same node without forming a cycle, as in a diamond: 0 -> 1 -> 3 and 0 -> 2 -> 3. Reaching node 3 a second time is harmless because it is already finished. A cycle exists only when DFS reaches a node that is still on the current path. Track three states: 0 unvisited, 1 on the current path, 2 finished.
payload.misconception: In a directed graph, reaching an already-visited node during DFS means there is a cycle.

metadata.concept: Remove nodes with in-degree 0 to get an order, and a cycle check for free

payload.concept: Remove nodes with in-degree 0 to get an order, and a cycle check for free
payload.example_bad:
// ... same loop ...
return order; // a partial order is returned for cyclic input
payload.explanation: Kahn's algorithm counts incoming edges for every node, queues the nodes with none, and repeatedly removes a queued node and decrements its neighbours' counts, queueing any that reach zero. The removal order is a valid topological order. Nodes on a cycle never reach zero, so if fewer than n nodes are removed the graph has a cycle. Build edges in the direction "must come first -> comes after"; for Course Schedule's [a, b] that is b -> a.
payload.misconception: Kahn's algorithm always returns a complete order.

metadata.concept: Union-find answers "are these connected?" as edges arrive

payload.complexity: Nearly O(1) amortised per operation (inverse Ackermann), O(n) space
payload.concept: Union-find answers "are these connected?" as edges arrive
payload.explanation: Union-find keeps each group as a tree identified by its root. Merging must connect the roots, not the nodes themselves, or groups are linked incorrectly. Path halving during find and attaching the smaller tree under the larger keep every operation nearly O(1). union returns false when both nodes already share a root, which means the new edge closes a cycle; counting successful unions gives the number of groups.
payload.misconception: Merging two groups means setting one node's parent to the other node.

JavaScript · grid · creation · L0
Concept: Every row of a grid must be its own array
Misconception: Array(m).fill(Array(n).fill(0)) creates an m x n grid of independent zeros.
Explanation: fill puts the same value into every slot. When that value is an array, every row is a reference to one shared array, so writing grid[1][1] changes every row. Create each row inside a callback, which runs once per row.
Incorrect:
const grid = Array(3).fill(Array(3).fill(0));
grid[1][1] = 5; // every row now has 5 in the middle
Correct:
const grid = Array.from({ length: 3 }, () => Array(3).fill(0));
grid[1][1] = 5; // only row 1 changes
Complexity: O(rows * cols)

payload.explanation: LeetCode passes boards such as Number of Islands as arrays of strings, '1' and '0'. === never converts types, so grid[r][c] === 1 is always false and the count stays 0. Compare with the string literal, or convert once with Number. Writing grid[r][c] = 0 mixes a number into a string board, and later checks against '0' then miss that cell. Java's char[][] boards have the same trap with '1' versus 1.

metadata.concept: Flood fill with an explicit stack, because recursion overflows on large regions

payload.complexity: O(rows * cols) time and heap space in the worst case
payload.concept: Flood fill with an explicit stack, because recursion overflows on large regions
payload.explanation: A recursive flood fill keeps one call-stack frame per cell on its current path. A large or snake-shaped region makes that path tens of thousands of cells long, past the roughly ten thousand frames Node allows, and the fill throws RangeError. An array used as a stack has no such limit. Mark each cell when it is pushed, so no cell is pushed twice.
payload.misconception: A recursive DFS flood fill works on any grid that fits in memory.

metadata.concept: Rotate a square matrix clockwise in place by transposing it and then reversing each row

payload.concept: Rotate a square matrix clockwise in place by transposing it and then reversing each row
payload.example_bad:
for (let r = 0; r < n; r++)
  for (let c = 0; c < n; c++) matrix[c][n - 1 - r] = matrix[r][c]; // overwrites unmoved cells
payload.explanation: Writing matrix[c][n - 1 - r] = matrix[r][c] overwrites a value before it has moved. Split the rotation into two moves that are each safe in place. Transposing swaps [r][c] with [c][r] for c > r only; looping over every pair swaps each one twice and changes nothing. Reversing every row then completes a clockwise turn. For anticlockwise, reverse the rows first and then transpose.
payload.misconception: Rotating in place means writing each cell straight to its new position.

JavaScript · heap · mental-model · L1
Concept: A heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array
Misconception: A heap's array is sorted, so the second-smallest value is at index 1 and the largest is at the end.
Explanation: A binary heap stores a complete binary tree level by level in an array. With zero-based indices, the children of i are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and the parent of i is at (i - 1) >> 1. The only rule is that each parent is no larger than its children in a min-heap. Siblings are unordered, so the second-smallest value is at index 1 or 2 and the largest is somewhere among the leaves.
Incorrect:
const heap = [1, 3, 2, 7, 4, 5, 6];
const secondSmallest = heap[1]; // 3, but the answer is 2
Correct:
const heap = [1, 3, 2, 7, 4, 5, 6];
const secondSmallest = Math.min(heap[1], heap[2]); // 2
Complexity: Index arithmetic is O(1); finding anything but the top is O(n)

JavaScript · heap · patterns · L3
Concept: The k largest live in a size-k min-heap
Misconception: To keep the k largest values, use a max-heap, because we want large values.
Explanation: A size-k heap must make it cheap to evict the weakest of the k items kept. For the k largest, the weakest is the smallest, which a min-heap keeps on top: compare each new value with the top and replace it if the new value is larger. A max-heap would evict the largest value instead. The same reasoning gives a max-heap for the k smallest or the k closest. Time is O(n log k) and memory O(k), which also works on streams.
Incorrect:
const h = new Heap((a, b) => b - a); // max-heap
for (const x of nums) { h.push(x); if (h.size > k) h.pop(); } // keeps the k smallest
Correct:
function kLargest(nums, k) {
  const h = new Heap((a, b) => a - b); // min-heap of the k largest so far
  for (const x of nums) { h.push(x); if (h.size > k) h.pop(); }
  return h; // its top is the k-th largest
}
Complexity: O(n log k) time, O(k) space

metadata.concept: Fast and slow pointers detect a cycle; compare the nodes with ===, not their values

payload.concept: Fast and slow pointers detect a cycle; compare the nodes with ===, not their values
payload.explanation: Values can repeat in a list with no cycle. A cycle means some node's next leads back to a node already passed. Move slow one step and fast two steps at a time; with a cycle, fast eventually lands on the same node object as slow, which === detects. If fast reaches null, there is no cycle. This uses O(1) memory, where a Set of visited nodes uses O(n).
payload.misconception: A list has a cycle when a value appears twice.

payload.concept: Two pointers kept n nodes apart find the nth node from the end in one pass
payload.explanation: Move a lead pointer n + 1 steps ahead of a trail pointer, starting both at a dummy node, then move them together until lead is null. trail then sits just before the node to remove. The dummy covers the case where the head itself is removed, which otherwise needs its own branch.
payload.misconception: Removing the nth node from the end needs one pass to count the length and a second to remove.

payload.example_bad:
const nodes = [];
for (let n = head; n; n = n.next) nodes.push(n); // O(n) extra memory
payload.explanation: Reorder List, Palindrome Linked List and similar problems split into steps already learned. Find the middle with fast and slow pointers, cut the list there, reverse the second half with the save-next loop, then weave or compare the two halves. Each step is O(n) time and O(1) space, so the whole solution is too. An array of nodes also works, but it costs O(n) extra memory.

In JavaScript, choose a linked list deliberately and rarely: when you hold references to nodes and must splice at them in O(1), when whole sublists move without copying, when versions share tails, or simply when the problem hands you `ListNode`. Misconception: Iterating with for...of or Array.from gives the characters a user sees.

Intl.Segmenter with granularity 'grapheme' splits text the way a reader sees it. Interview problems rarely need this, but reversing or truncating user-facing text does.

const s = '👍🏽!';
const seg = new Intl.Segmenter('en', { granularity: 'grapheme' });
const graphemes = Array.from(seg.segment(s), x => x.segment); // ['👍🏽', '!']
const reversed = graphemes.reverse().join('');                  // '!👍🏽'
Complexity: O(n)
