Encode the pair as a primitive instead, either as a string such as `${r},${c}` or as a number r * cols + c when the column count is known. Numbers are faster and use less memory, and strings work for any shape. Java uses a record for the same job.
payload.misconception: seen.has([r, c]) finds a cell that was added as [r, c] earlier.

metadata.concept: Intersect two sets by iterating the smaller one and checking the larger one

payload.complexity: O(min(n, m)) for intersection, O(n + m) for union
payload.concept: Intersect two sets by iterating the smaller one and checking the larger one
payload.example_bad:
const a = [1, 2, 3, 4], b = [3, 4, 5];
const common = a.filter(x => b.includes(x)); // O(n * m)
payload.explanation: a.filter(x => b.includes(x)) is O(n * m). Iterate the smaller set and keep the values the larger set has, which is O(min(n, m)). Union is new Set([...a, ...b]), and difference keeps the values of a that b lacks. Node 22 and current browsers also have a.intersection(b), a.union(b) and a.difference(b), which return new sets, but check the judge's runtime before relying on them.
payload.misconception: Set operations need both sets turned into arrays and combined with filter and includes.

metadata.concept: Use push and pop on the end of an array as a stack, with the top at arr[arr.length - 1]

payload.complexity: O(1) for push, pop and peek
payload.concept: Use push and pop on the end of an array as a stack, with the top at arr[arr.length - 1]
payload.explanation: push and pop work on the end of the array in O(1). unshift and shift work on the front and move every element, which is O(n). Peek with stack[stack.length - 1] or stack.at(-1). Check stack.length before popping, because pop on an empty array returns undefined instead of throwing, which hides bugs.
payload.misconception: unshift and shift work just as well for a stack.

metadata.concept: Reach for a stack when the newest unfinished item must be resolved first

payload.concept: Reach for a stack when the newest unfinished item must be resolved first
payload.explanation: A stack fits whenever the most recent open item is the next one to close: matching brackets, evaluating postfix expressions, undoing moves, replacing recursion and finding the next greater element. Ask whether each new item resolves the newest pending one. If it does, push pending items and pop them as they are resolved.
payload.misconception: A stack is only for undo and for matching parentheses.

metadata.concept: A monotonic stack of indexes finds every next greater element in one O(n) pass

payload.concept: A monotonic stack of indexes finds every next greater element in one O(n) pass
payload.explanation: Keep a stack of indexes whose answer is still unknown, with their values decreasing from bottom to top. When a larger value arrives, it is the answer for every smaller value on top, so pop them and record it. Each index is pushed and popped once, so the whole pass is O(n). Store indexes rather than values when the answer is a distance.
payload.misconception: Finding the next greater element for every position needs a nested loop.

metadata.concept: Dequeue by advancing a head index, because shift is O(n)

payload.concept: Dequeue by advancing a head index, because shift is O(n)
payload.explanation: Arrays have no O(1) way to remove the first element. shift moves every remaining element, so a BFS over n nodes that uses shift can take O(n^2). Keep a head index instead: read queue[head++], and treat the queue as empty when head equals queue.length. The array is freed when the BFS ends; a long-running queue should compact itself or use a ring buffer.
payload.misconception: queue.shift() is O(1) because arrays work as queues.

metadata.concept: Put every source in the queue at distance 0, then run one BFS

payload.concept: Put every source in the queue at distance 0, then run one BFS
payload.example_bad: for (const [r, c] of sources) bfsFrom(r, c); // O(sources * cells)
payload.explanation: One BFS per source costs O(sources * cells). Put all the sources in the queue at the start, at distance 0, and run a single BFS. The first time a cell is reached, it is reached from its nearest source. Rotting Oranges counts the levels this way, and Walls and Gates writes each distance into the grid.
payload.misconception: To find each cell's distance to its nearest source, run a separate BFS from each source.

metadata.concept: A linked list is a chain of node objects, and variables hold references to nodes, not copies

payload.concept: A linked list is a chain of node objects, and variables hold references to nodes, not copies
payload.explanation: A node is an object with val and next, and the list ends where next is null. let curr = head makes curr point at the same node as head, so curr.val = 99 or curr.next = x changes the list everyone sees. curr = curr.next only moves that one variable along the chain and leaves the list unchanged.
payload.misconception: Assigning a node to a new variable makes a copy of it.

metadata.concept: Walk a list with while (curr), and check a pointer before reading its next

payload.concept: Walk a list with while (curr), and check a pointer before reading its next
payload.example_bad:
let curr = head;
while (curr.next) { sum += curr.val; curr = curr.next; } // misses the tail; throws when head is null
payload.explanation: while (curr.next) stops at the last node without processing it, and throws on an empty list because reading next from null is a TypeError. while (curr) visits every node, including the last, and handles a null head. A fast pointer that jumps two nodes must check fast && fast.next before each jump.
payload.misconception: while (curr.next) visits every node in the list.

metadata.concept: A dummy node before the head removes the special case for the first node

payload.complexity: O(n + m) time, O(1) extra space
payload.concept: A dummy node before the head removes the special case for the first node
payload.explanation: When the head itself may be removed, or the result list starts empty, start from const dummy = new ListNode(0, head) and keep a tail or prev pointer. Every node, including the first, then has a node before it, so one rule handles every position. Return dummy.next at the end.
payload.misconception: Code that builds or edits a list needs a separate branch for the first node.

metadata.concept: Check both bounds before indexing a grid, and loop over a directions array for neighbours

payload.concept: Check both bounds before indexing a grid, and loop over a directions array for neighbours
payload.example_bad: if (grid[r - 1][c] === 1) visit(r - 1, c); // TypeError when r is 0
payload.explanation: grid[-1] is undefined, and reading [c] from undefined throws a TypeError, so a bad row index crashes while a bad column index silently returns undefined. Check 0 <= r < rows and 0 <= c < cols before every read. A constant array of [dr, dc] pairs replaces four copied branches, and moving to eight directions only changes that array.
payload.misconception: grid[r][c] with an out-of-range r just returns undefined, so bounds checks are optional.

metadata.concept: A binary tree node has val, left and right, and null is an empty subtree rather than an error

payload.concept: A binary tree node has val, left and right, and null is an empty subtree rather than an error
payload.explanation: Each node holds a value and two references, each either a node or null. Treat null as the empty tree: most functions are simplest when the base case handles null, and then leaves need no branch of their own. LeetCode writes trees level by level, as in [3, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7], where null marks a missing child.
payload.misconception: A leaf is a special case, so tree code must check for leaves before recursing.

metadata.concept: Preorder, inorder and postorder differ only in where the node itself is visited

payload.concept: Preorder, inorder and postorder differ only in where the node itself is visited
payload.explanation: All three recurse into the left subtree and then the right. Preorder visits the node before its children, inorder between them and postorder after them. Preorder copies or serialises a tree, inorder lists a BST in sorted order, and postorder computes answers that need both children first, such as height. Push into one shared result array instead of concatenating arrays at every level.
payload.misconception: The three depth-first orders need three different algorithms.

metadata.concept: In a BST every value in the left subtree is smaller than the node and every value in the right subtree is larger

payload.complexity: O(h) per search or insert; h is about log n when balanced and n when skewed
payload.concept: In a BST every value in the left subtree is smaller than the node and every value in the right subtree is larger
payload.explanation: The rule covers whole subtrees, not just children: a node's right subtree may not contain anything smaller than the node, however deep it is. That rule is what lets search, insert and lowest common ancestor go down one side only, in O(h). State the policy for duplicates; most problems allow none.
payload.misconception: A tree is a BST when each node is larger than its left child and smaller than its right child.

metadata.concept: A complete binary tree fills every level from left to right, so it fits in an array with no gaps

payload.concept: A complete binary tree fills every level from left to right, so it fits in an array with no gaps
payload.explanation: A tree where every node has zero or two children is called full. A complete tree has every level full except possibly the last, which is filled from the left. Because it has no gaps, its nodes can be numbered level by level and stored in an array, with the children of node i at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2. That is why a heap needs no node objects, and why its height is floor(log2 n).
payload.misconception: A complete binary tree is one where every node has zero or two children.

metadata.concept: Return what the parent can extend, and record the best answer that bends through each node in an outer variable

payload.concept: Return what the parent can extend, and record the best answer that bends through each node in an outer variable
payload.explanation: In problems such as diameter, the best path can bend through a node and use both children, but a parent can only extend one downward branch. So the function returns the best single branch, which the parent can use, and at each node updates an outer variable with the bent path through that node. Returning the bent path to the parent is the usual bug.
payload.misconception: The value a recursive call returns must be the final answer for that subtree.

metadata.concept: Pass information about the path down as an argument, not in a shared variable

payload.concept: Pass information about the path down as an argument, not in a shared variable
payload.explanation: Information from ancestors, such as the largest value on the path, the depth or the bounds a BST allows, belongs to one path only. A shared outer variable carries values from a left branch into its right sibling unless it is carefully restored. Passing the value as a parameter gives each call its own copy, and returning from the call restores it automatically.
payload.misconception: The largest value seen so far on the path can be kept in one outer variable during DFS.

metadata.concept: An inorder traversal of a BST visits values in ascending order, so it can stop early

payload.concept: An inorder traversal of a BST visits values in ascending order, so it can stop early
payload.explanation: Inorder visits the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree, which in a BST is ascending order. Counting during the traversal finds the k-th smallest value in O(h + k) and stops as soon as it gets there. The same property validates a BST, since each value must be larger than the one visited before it.
payload.misconception: Finding the k-th smallest value in a BST means collecting every value and sorting.

metadata.concept: An explicit stack replaces recursion; push the right child before the left for preorder

payload.concept: An explicit stack replaces recursion; push the right child before the left for preorder
payload.explanation: A stack pops the last item pushed, so preorder pushes the right child first to process the left one first. Inorder walks left while pushing each node, then pops a node, visits it and moves to its right child. Iteration avoids the call-stack limit on very deep, skewed trees, which in Node is often around ten thousand frames.
payload.misconception: Iterative preorder pushes the left child and then the right child.

metadata.concept: push sifts the new last element up, and pop moves the last element to the root and sifts it down

payload.complexity: O(log n) per push or pop
payload.concept: push sifts the new last element up, and pop moves the last element to the root and sifts it down
payload.example_bad:
// Removing the top with shift is O(n), and the array is no longer a heap.
const top = heap.shift();
payload.explanation: Promoting children leaves a hole that breaks the complete shape. Instead, pop swaps the root with the last element, removes it, and sifts the new root down, swapping it with its smaller child until neither child is smaller. push appends at the end and swaps with the parent while the new value is smaller. Each operation follows one path from the root to a leaf, so it is O(log n).
payload.misconception: After the top is removed, the smaller child simply moves up to replace it.

metadata.concept: JavaScript has no built-in priority queue, so write one small Heap class that takes a comparator

payload.complexity: O(log n) for push and pop, O(1) for peek and size
payload.concept: JavaScript has no built-in priority queue, so write one small Heap class that takes a comparator
payload.example_bad:
const pq = [];
function push(x) { pq.push(x); pq.sort((a, b) => a - b); } // O(n log n) per push
payload.explanation: JavaScript has no built-in heap, so solutions either write one or use one the platform provides; LeetCode's JavaScript runtime includes @datastructures-js/priority-queue. The other heap and graph chunks use this API: new Heap(compare), where compare(a, b) below 0 means a comes out first, plus push, pop, peek and a size getter. Sorting after every push costs O(n log n) per push instead of O(log n).
payload.misconception: Sorting the array after every push is a good enough priority queue.

metadata.concept: An indexed heap supports decrease-key by tracking where each item sits in the array

payload.complexity: O(log n) per push, pop and decreaseKey; O(n) space
payload.concept: An indexed heap supports decrease-key by tracking where each item sits in the array
payload.explanation: With lazy deletion the heap can grow to O(E) entries. When it must hold one entry per item, for example on a dense graph or in a scheduler that changes priorities often, keep a Map from each item to its array index and update it on every swap. After a priority changes, sift that index up or down. Each update is O(log n), and the heap never holds more than n entries.
payload.misconception: Lazy deletion is always good enough, so a heap never needs decrease-key.

metadata.concept: A trie stores strings one character per edge, so words that share a prefix share nodes

payload.complexity: O(m) per insert or lookup for a word of length m
payload.concept: A trie stores strings one character per edge, so words that share a prefix share nodes
payload.example_bad:
const words = ['car', 'card', 'care'];
const hasPrefix = p => words.some(w => w.startsWith(p)); // scans every word on each query
payload.explanation: Each node holds a map from the next character to a child node. Inserting a word walks from the root one character at a time and creates the children that are missing. All words with the same prefix pass through the same node, so checking a prefix of length m costs O(m) however many words are stored. A flag on a node marks where a word ends.
payload.misconception: A trie stores whole words inside its nodes.

metadata.concept: For autocomplete, walk to the prefix node, then DFS in sorted child order and stop after k words

payload.complexity: O(prefix length + nodes visited before k words are found)
payload.concept: For autocomplete, walk to the prefix node, then DFS in sorted child order and stop after k words
payload.explanation: After walking the prefix, only that node's subtree matters. A DFS that visits children in alphabetical order produces words in lexicographic order, so it can stop as soon as it has k words. When there are many queries, storing the top suggestions on each node at insert time makes each query O(prefix length). Search Suggestions System asks for three words per typed prefix.
payload.misconception: Autocomplete must collect every word under the prefix and then sort them.

metadata.concept: Before coding a graph problem, decide on direction, weights, node names and whether cycles or several components can occur

payload.concept: Before coding a graph problem, decide on direction, weights, node names and whether cycles or several components can occur
payload.example_bad:
// Treats prerequisites as undirected, but [course, pre] means pre -> course only.
for (const [course, pre] of prerequisites) { adj[course].push(pre); adj[pre].push(course); }
payload.explanation: Interview inputs give graphs as an edge list such as [[0, 1], [1, 2]], as an adjacency list, as a grid, or implicitly, as words one letter apart. Before coding, answer four questions. Are edges one-way or two-way? Do they have weights? Are the nodes 0 to n - 1 or arbitrary keys? Can there be cycles or several components? Each answer changes the representation and the algorithm.
payload.misconception: Every graph problem hands you a ready-made graph data structure.

metadata.concept: Build an adjacency list with one array per node, using Array.from for numbered nodes and a Map for named ones

payload.concept: Build an adjacency list with one array per node, using Array.from for numbered nodes and a Map for named ones
payload.example_bad: const adj = Array(n).fill([]); // one shared array for every node
payload.explanation: A matrix uses O(V^2) memory and makes listing a node's neighbours O(V), even when the graph is sparse. An adjacency list uses O(V + E) and lists only real neighbours. For nodes 0 to n - 1, use Array.from({ length: n }, () => []). For string or sparse ids, use a Map whose values start as empty arrays. Store [neighbour, weight] pairs when the edges have weights.
payload.misconception: An adjacency matrix is the default way to store a graph.

metadata.concept: Iterative DFS uses an array as a stack and marks each node as seen when it is pushed

payload.concept: Iterative DFS uses an array as a stack and marks each node as seen when it is pushed
payload.explanation: Without a visited set, a cycle pushes the same nodes forever, and shared neighbours are pushed many times. Mark a node as seen when it is pushed, or skip seen nodes when they are popped, and use one rule consistently. An explicit stack avoids stack overflow on deep graphs such as a chain of 100,000 nodes. It suits reachability and components, but post-order work such as cycle detection needs extra state.
payload.misconception: A DFS loop with a stack needs no visited set, because each node is popped only once.

metadata.concept: Start a new traversal from every node not yet seen, because one traversal covers only one component

payload.concept: Start a new traversal from every node not yet seen, because one traversal covers only one component
payload.explanation: A traversal reaches only the nodes connected to where it starts. Graphs in interview problems are often disconnected, so wrap the traversal in an outer loop over every node and start a new one from each node not yet seen. The number of starts is the number of components, and the whole loop is still O(V + E) because each node is visited once.
payload.misconception: A DFS from node 0 visits the whole graph.

metadata.concept: Kruskal sorts edges by weight and keeps each edge that joins two different components

payload.complexity: O(E log E) time, O(V) space
payload.concept: Kruskal sorts edges by weight and keeps each edge that joins two different components
payload.example_bad:
// Keeps each node's cheapest edge: can leave the graph in several pieces.
const chosen = adj.map(list => list.reduce((best, e) => (e[1] < best[1] ? e : best)));
payload.explanation: Each node's cheapest edge can leave the graph in several pieces. Kruskal sorts all the edges by weight and keeps each one whose ends are in different components, which union-find answers in nearly O(1). It stops after n - 1 edges. For dense inputs given as points, such as Min Cost to Connect All Points, Prim's algorithm with an O(n^2) loop avoids building all n^2 edges.
payload.misconception: Taking every node's cheapest edge always produces a minimum spanning tree.

metadata.concept: Map keys match by SameValueZero, not by contents

payload.complexity: O(1) average per get, set and has, plus the cost of building the key
payload.concept: Map keys match by SameValueZero, not by contents
payload.explanation: Map compares keys with SameValueZero: primitives by value (NaN equals NaN, 0 equals -0), objects and arrays only by reference. Each array literal is a new object, so a key built from [r, c] never matches a later [r, c]. Encode composite keys as strings or nest Maps.
payload.misconception: Two arrays or objects with the same contents are the same Map key.

payload.answer: A Map, because its keys are node objects and a Map keys them by identity, while an object would turn every node into the same '[object Object]' key.
payload.prompt: Clone Graph needs original node -> copy. Object or Map? One sentence why.

metadata.concept: Count with m.set(k, (m.get(k) ?? 0) + 1), and delete keys whose count falls to zero

payload.concept: Count with m.set(k, (m.get(k) ?? 0) + 1), and delete keys whose count falls to zero
payload.example_bad:
const count = new Map();
for (const c of 'aab') count.set(c, count.get(c) + 1); // every count is NaN
payload.explanation: get returns undefined for a new key, and undefined + 1 is NaN, which then stays NaN however many times the key is counted. Default with ?? 0. In sliding windows, delete a key when its count drops to 0, so that m.size still equals the number of distinct keys in the window. Java's equivalent is merge(k, 1, Integer::sum).
payload.misconception: m.set(k, m.get(k) + 1) works for a key that has not been seen yet.

metadata.concept: Group values by creating each group's array once and pushing into it

payload.complexity: O(n * k log k) for Group Anagrams with sorted keys of length k
payload.concept: Group values by creating each group's array once and pushing into it
payload.explanation: Spreading the old group into a new array copies the whole group on every append, so a group of k items costs O(k^2) to build. Create the array once when the key is new, then push into it. When every item is available up front, Map.groupBy (ES2024, Node 21 and later) builds the whole grouping in one call.
payload.misconception: m.set(key, [...(m.get(key) ?? []), value]) is a fine way to add a value to a group.

metadata.concept: JavaScript has no TreeMap, so keep keys in a sorted array and binary search it for floor and ceiling queries

payload.complexity: O(1) amortised per set and O(log n) per get
payload.concept: JavaScript has no TreeMap, so keep keys in a sorted array and binary search it for floor and ceiling queries
payload.example_bad:
let best = '';
for (const [t, v] of history) if (t <= time) best = v; // O(n) per query
payload.explanation: A Map keeps insertion order, not sorted order, and has no floor or ceiling lookup. When keys arrive in increasing order, as timestamps do in Time Based Key-Value Store, append them to an array and binary search it in O(log n). When they arrive in any order, keep the array sorted with a binary-search insert, which costs O(n) per insert, or use a balanced tree library. Java solves the same problem with TreeMap.floorEntry.
payload.misconception: A Map can answer "largest key at or below t" because it keeps its keys in order.

JavaScript · object · equality · L1
Concept: === compares objects by reference, so compare the fields you need or map each object to a key
Misconception: Two objects with the same fields are ===, and includes finds a matching object.
Explanation: An object literal creates a new object every time, so { x: 1 } === { x: 1 } is false, and includes or indexOf with a freshly built object always misses. JavaScript has no equals or hashCode to override, unlike Java. Compare the fields you care about, keep a reference to the original object, or map each object to a primitive key such as `${p.x},${p.y}` before putting it in a Set or Map.
Incorrect:
const points = [{ x: 1, y: 2 }];
points.includes({ x: 1, y: 2 }); // false
Correct:
const a = { x: 1, y: 2 }, b = { x: 1, y: 2 };
const sameRef = a === b;                       // false
const sameFields = a.x === b.x && a.y === b.y; // true
const key = p => `${p.x},${p.y}`;
const seen = new Set([key(a)]);
const found = seen.has(key(b));                // true
Complexity: O(fields) per comparison; O(1) average per Set lookup

JavaScript · object · edge-cases · L1
Concept: Use ?? for defaults and ?. for optional access, because || also replaces 0 and ''
Misconception: x || fallback only replaces values that are missing.
Explanation: || replaces every falsy value: 0, '', NaN, false, null and undefined. A memoised answer of 0 or an empty string then turns into the fallback, which breaks DP and counting code. ?? replaces only null and undefined. ?. stops at null or undefined and returns undefined instead of throwing, which suits optional children, but used everywhere it can hide real bugs.
Incorrect:
const memo = { 3: 0 };
const ways = memo[3] || -1; // -1, although 0 was stored
Correct:
const memo = { 3: 0 };
const ways = memo[3] ?? -1;            // 0
const missing = memo[4] ?? -1;         // -1
const node = { left: null };
const leftVal = node.left?.val ?? 0;   // 0, and no TypeError
Complexity: O(1)

JavaScript · JavaScript Objects · Key handling track
Keys are the object's equivalent of array indices, and most object bugs are key bugs: a key that was silently converted, a key that already existed on the prototype, or a key that exists with a falsy value. Each row is one lesson; the typical bug is the misconception to target and the technique is the exit skill.

JavaScript · JavaScript Objects · Object model track
Every object has a hidden half: the prototype it inherits from, the attributes of each property, and the `this` its methods depend on. This track teaches that half, because it explains the strange results in the key-handling track and it underpins every design-class problem (Implement Trie, Find Median from Data Stream, the Serialize/Deserialize codec).

Safe technique: `Object.create(null)` for pure data maps; note it then has no `toString` for templating

Prompt: Binary Tree Right Side View: BFS with level snapshots, or DFS with depth? One sentence each way.

payload.answer: BFS: process each level with a snapshot and keep its last node. DFS: visit right before left and record a node whenever its depth equals the number of values found so far. Both are O(n).
payload.prompt: Binary Tree Right Side View: BFS with level snapshots, or DFS with depth? One sentence each way.

metadata.concept: BFS reaches every node first along a shortest path when each edge costs 1

payload.concept: BFS reaches every node first along a shortest path when each edge costs 1
payload.explanation: BFS leaves nodes in order of their distance from the start, so the first time a node is queued, its distance is final: record dist[v] = dist[u] + 1 at that moment. DFS finds a path, not necessarily the shortest, and exploring every path to compare them is exponential. With weighted edges, BFS no longer works and Dijkstra's algorithm is needed.
payload.misconception: A DFS that explores every path finds shortest paths just as well as BFS.

metadata.concept: A fixed-size circular array gives O(1) enqueue and dequeue and reuses its slots

payload.concept: A fixed-size circular array gives O(1) enqueue and dequeue and reuses its slots
payload.explanation: With a head index, the slots before head are never reused, so a queue that runs forever keeps growing even when it holds few items. A ring buffer stores items in a fixed array and wraps both ends with modulo: the tail slot is (head + size) % capacity. Track size separately, because head === tail happens both when the buffer is empty and when it is full.
payload.misconception: A head index into a growing array is a good queue for a long-running stream.

metadata.concept: Keep a deque of indexes with decreasing values, so the window maximum is always at the front

payload.complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space for the index array
payload.concept: Keep a deque of indexes with decreasing values, so the window maximum is always at the front
payload.example_bad:
const out = [];
for (let i = 0; i + k <= nums.length; i++) out.push(Math.max(...nums.slice(i, i + k))); // O(n * k)
payload.explanation: Once a larger value arrives, smaller values before it can never be a window maximum, so drop them from the back. Once an index leaves the window, drop it from the front. An array with a head index works as the deque: advance head for the front, pop for the back. Each index enters and leaves once, so the pass is O(n) instead of O(n * k).
payload.misconception: The maximum of each sliding window has to be found by scanning the window.

JavaScript · JavaScript Queues and Deques · When it must be a queue or deque, and when to use something else
Use a queue when the oldest waiting item must go next: fairness, level-by-level order, and the shortest path in steps all depend on it. Use a deque when both ends change, most often to keep a window's extremes. Use something else when the next item is the most recent (stack), the most urgent (heap), or when a plain loop over a fixed list is enough.

payload.concept: Set.prototype.add returns the set, not a boolean, so it cannot test for a duplicate
payload.explanation: Java's Set.add returns false when the element was already present. JavaScript's add returns the Set itself, which is always truthy, so that condition never fires and duplicates pass silently. Check has before add, or compare size before and after the add. delete, by contrast, does return a boolean.

payload.concept: A Set iterates in insertion order, not sorted order, so use has to find neighbours instead of sorting
payload.example_bad:
const set = new Set([3, 1, 2]);
const smallest = [...set][0]; // 3: the first value added, not the smallest
payload.explanation: Sets and Maps iterate in the order values were first added, and JavaScript has no built-in sorted set. When sorted output is needed, spread and sort with a numeric comparator in O(n log n). Often order is not needed at all: Longest Consecutive Sequence finds each run's start with has(x - 1) and counts upwards with has, which is O(n) overall.
payload.misconception: A Set keeps its values sorted, like Java's TreeSet.

metadata.concept: A Number bitmask has 32 usable bits; the sign bit requires careful interpretation and shift-based subset loop bounds have a narrower domain
metadata.correction_review: 2026-10-18 specific claim review; not whole-record certification

payload.complexity: O(1) per bit operation; O(2^n * n) to list every subset
payload.concept: A Number bitmask has 32 usable bits; the sign bit requires careful interpretation and shift-based subset loop bounds have a narrower domain
payload.explanation: Bit i of an integer can record whether i is in a set: add with mask | (1 << i) and test with (mask >> i) & 1. JavaScript converts both operands to 32-bit signed integers and takes the shift count modulo 32, so 1 << 31 is negative and 1 << 32 is 1. Bit 31 is usable as a flag even though the Number result is signed; test membership with a nonzero bitwise result, not a positive-result check. The subset loop below requires 0 <= nums.length <= 30 because its bound uses a signed left shift; practical enumeration requires much smaller inputs. For wider sets, use BigInt (1n << 40n) or an array of booleans. Enumerating all masks from 0 to 2^n - 1 lists every subset.
payload.misconception: 1 << 32 sets bit 32 of a mask.

JavaScript · JavaScript Sets · Set algebra track
Sets combine through algebra: JavaScript added the operations as built-in methods in ES2025 (shipped across major browsers in 2024 and in Node 22), and learners should know both the built-ins and the manual versions older runtimes need. Use a Set when the only question is membership and the universe of possible values is large, sparse or unknown. JavaScript · stack · iteration · L1
Concept: An array stack keeps its top at the end, so it prints and iterates from bottom to top
Misconception: Iterating a stack array with for...of visits items from the top down.
Explanation: for...of, forEach, join and console.log all start at index 0, which is the bottom of an array stack. To read from the top, loop from length - 1 down to 0, or take a reversed copy with toReversed() (ES2023) without changing the stack. Problems that return the stack's contents, such as Simplify Path, usually want bottom-to-top, which is the natural order. Java's ArrayDeque is the opposite: it iterates from the top.
Incorrect:
const stack = ['a', 'b', 'c']; // 'c' is the top
for (const item of stack) console.log(item); // a, b, c: bottom first
Correct:
const stack = [];
stack.push('a'); stack.push('b'); stack.push('c');
const bottomUp = stack.join('/'); // 'a/b/c'
const topDown = [];
for (let i = stack.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) topDown.push(stack[i]); // ['c', 'b', 'a']
Complexity: O(n) to iterate

payload.concept: Store the running minimum beside each item so getMin stays O(1) after pops
payload.explanation: After the minimum is popped, one variable cannot recover the previous minimum without scanning the whole stack. Keep a second stack in which entry i is the minimum of the first i + 1 items. push stores min(x, previous minimum), and pop removes from both, so push, pop, top and getMin are all O(1). Private # fields keep outside code from breaking the pairing.
payload.misconception: A single variable holding the minimum is enough for a stack with getMin.

metadata.concept: In postfix evaluation the right operand pops first, and division truncates toward zero

payload.concept: In postfix evaluation the right operand pops first, and division truncates toward zero
payload.example_bad:
const a = stack.pop(), b = stack.pop();
stack.push(a - b); // ["4", "1", "-"] gives -3 instead of 3
payload.explanation: The right operand was pushed last, so it comes off the stack first: pop b, then pop a, then compute a op b. Addition and multiplication hide the mistake; subtraction and division expose it. Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation truncates division toward zero, so use Math.trunc(a / b). Math.floor rounds negative results down and gives the wrong answer.

document:
JavaScript · string · equality · L1
Concept: === compares string contents, but < and the default sort compare UTF-16 code units
Misconception: Comparing strings with < or sorting them with sort() puts them in dictionary order.
Explanation: Unlike Java's ==, === compares the text of two strings, so a string built at runtime equals a literal with the same characters. < and the default sort compare code units one at a time, so every uppercase letter comes before every lowercase one and numeric strings sort as text: '10' comes before '9'. Use localeCompare for human order and convert with Number for numeric order. A sorted copy of a word is a handy anagram key.
Incorrect:
['b', 'C', 'a'].sort();   // ['C', 'a', 'b']
['10', '9', '2'].sort();  // ['10', '2', '9']
Correct:
const same = 'ab' === ['a', 'b'].join('');                         // true
const words = ['b', 'C', 'a'].sort((x, y) => x.localeCompare(y));  // ['a', 'b', 'C']
const nums = ['10', '9', '2'].sort((x, y) => Number(x) - Number(y)); // ['2', '9', '10']
const key = [...'eat'].sort().join('');                            // 'aet'
Complexity: O(n) per comparison of two strings of length n

Concept: split with a string separator matches it literally and keeps every empty field
Misconception: s.split(' ') splits a sentence into its words.
Explanation: Each separator produces a field boundary, so repeated, leading or trailing spaces give empty strings: '  the sky '.split(' ') has empty entries. Trim and split on the regex /\s+/ to get words. A string separator is matched literally, so '.' splits on dots, unlike Java's regex-based split, and trailing empty fields are kept, also unlike Java. split('') splits into code units, so use [...s] when emoji may appear.
Incorrect:
const words = '  the sky  '.split(' '); // ['', '', 'the', 'sky', '', '']
Correct:
const words = '  the sky  '.trim().split(/\s+/); // ['the', 'sky']
const fields = 'a,b,,'.split(',');               // ['a', 'b', '', '']
const parts = 'a.b.c'.split('.');                // ['a', 'b', 'c']
Complexity: O(n)

JavaScript · JavaScript Strings · Unicode track
A JavaScript "character" exists at three levels: UTF-16 code units (what `length` and `s[i]` see), code points (what `for...of` sees) and graphemes (what a person sees). Most interview problems promise lowercase English letters, so ASCII techniques are correct there, but every learner should know where they stop being correct.

```javascript
const s = 'e\u0301\u{1F44D}\u{1F3FD}';      // "é👍🏽": e + combining accent, thumbs up + skin tone
s.length;                                   // 6 UTF-16 code units
[...s].length;                              // 4 code points
const seg = new Intl.Segmenter('en', { granularity: 'grapheme' });
[...seg.segment(s)].length;                 // 2 user-perceived characters
s.normalize('NFC').length;                  // 5: e + accent becomes one code point
```

metadata.concept: Every recursive tree function has a three-part contract

payload.concept: Every recursive tree function has a three-part contract
payload.explanation: A recursive function on a binary tree must decide three things before any code is written: what it returns for null (the answer for an empty tree), what it passes down to each child, and what it returns up to its parent. Most binary-tree bugs break one of these. Writing the contract as a one-line comment first makes the base case and the use of the children's results explicit.
payload.misconception: A recursive tree function only has to visit every node; what it returns can be worked out later.

metadata.concept: A BST check must pass value bounds down the whole path

payload.concept: A BST check must pass value bounds down the whole path
payload.explanation: The BST rule applies to whole subtrees, not just children: every value in a node's right subtree must be larger than the node, including grandchildren. Checking only children accepts [5, 4, 6, null, null, 3, 7], where 3 sits in 5's right subtree. Pass an open interval (low, high) down the recursion: going left narrows high to the node's value, going right narrows low.
payload.misconception: A binary tree is a valid BST if every node is larger than its left child and smaller than its right child.

payload.explanation: Preorder handles a node before its children: use it for copying, serialising and decisions made on the way down. Inorder visits a BST in sorted order: use it for the k-th smallest value or checking order. Postorder handles a node after both children: use it whenever the answer needs the children's results, such as height, balance or path sums. Level order groups nodes by depth: use it for per-level output or the rightmost node of each level. Choosing the wrong order usually means extra sorting or a second pass.
payload.misconception: Any traversal works as long as every node is visited.

metadata.concept: Return one branch upward, record the two-branch path globally

payload.concept: Return one branch upward, record the two-branch path globally
payload.explanation: A path can bend at most once. At each node, the best path that bends there is node.val plus the best non-negative gain from each side; record it in a global maximum. The parent can only extend one side, so return node.val plus the larger gain. Negative gains are dropped with Math.max(0, ...). The global maximum starts at -Infinity because the path must contain at least one node, so an all-negative tree returns its largest single value.
payload.misconception: The function can return the best path through a node, including both children, and an empty path (sum 0) is a valid answer.

JavaScript · JavaScript Binary Trees · Recursion contract track
Every recursive tree function has a contract with three clauses: what it returns for `null`, what it passes down to its children, and what it returns up to its parent. Most tree bugs break one clause, and four shapes cover almost every Blind 75 tree problem: return up (height), pass down (bounds or path state), combine children plus a global answer (diameter, maximum path sum), and compare two trees in step (Same Tree). Each row is one lesson.

metadata.concept: A path is a prefix; only an end marker makes it a word

payload.complexity: O(L) per call, where L is the string length
payload.concept: A path is a prefix; only an end marker makes it a word
payload.explanation: In a trie every node on a path represents a prefix, and inserting "car" creates nodes for "c", "ca" and "car". Only the last node gets an end marker. search must therefore walk the path and check the marker, while startsWith only needs the path to exist. With only "car" stored, search('ca') is false and startsWith('ca') is true.
payload.misconception: If the walk for a string reaches a node, the string is a stored word.

metadata.concept: Keep children in a Map, separate from the node's flags

payload.complexity: O(segments) per insert; one Map per node
payload.concept: Keep children in a Map, separate from the node's flags
payload.explanation: A plain object inherits keys such as constructor, so a trie over words or path segments can find segments that were never inserted. Mixing flags like end into the same object also breaks as soon as a segment is called "end". Give each node a children Map and separate fields for its flags. Use Array(26) only when every character is guaranteed to be a lowercase letter; it is fast and keeps alphabetical order, but wastes memory on sparse tries.
payload.misconception: A plain object can hold both a node's children and its flags, keyed by character.

metadata.concept: A wildcard branches into every child; a letter follows one

payload.complexity: O(L) with no wildcards; up to O(nodes) when the pattern is mostly wildcards
payload.concept: A wildcard branches into every child; a letter follows one
payload.explanation: When the pattern has '.', any child may lead to a match, so the search must try each child and succeed if any of them succeeds. Returning inside the loop stops after the first child even when it fails. Letters follow exactly one child, or fail if it is missing. At the end of the pattern the current node must be an end node. A pattern of only dots can visit every node down to its length, which is the worst case.
payload.misconception: At a wildcard, returning the result of the first child's search is enough.

metadata.concept: Search the board once while walking a trie, and prune finished branches

payload.complexity: O(m · n · 4 · 3^(L-1)) worst case; pruning removes most of it in practice
payload.concept: Search the board once while walking a trie, and prune finished branches
payload.example_bad:
// One full board search per word: shared prefixes are explored again and again.
return words.filter(w => existsOnBoard(board, w));
payload.explanation: Running a separate board search per word repeats the same paths for every word that shares a prefix. Build a trie of the words, store each word on its end node, and run one DFS from every cell that walks the board and the trie together. Report a word when its end node is reached, then clear it so it is reported once. JavaScript · JavaScript Tries · Node and path track
Every trie operation walks one path from the root, one character per level, and every trie bug is a mistake about that path: creating nodes that already exist, stopping without checking the end marker, or deleting nodes another word still needs.

[Diagram: trie for car, cat, cart, do, dog]

The path for "ca" exists, so `startsWith('ca')` is true, but no word ends at its `a` node, so `search('ca')` is false.

metadata.concept: A group is identified by its root, so union and connectivity both work on roots

payload.concept: A group is identified by its root, so union and connectivity both work on roots
payload.example_bad:
function union(a, b) { parent[a] = b; }
function connected(a, b) { return parent[a] === parent[b]; }
payload.explanation: Union-find stores each group as a tree in a parent array, and only the root, the node that is its own parent, identifies the group. Setting parent[a] = b moves only a and leaves the rest of a's group behind. Two members of one group can have different direct parents, so comparing parent[a] with parent[b] gives false negatives. Always call find on both sides, link one root under the other, and compare roots.
payload.misconception: parent[a] = b merges a's and b's groups, and parent[a] === parent[b] means they are connected.

metadata.concept: Path compression plus union by size make union-find nearly O(1) per operation

payload.complexity: Nearly O(1) amortised per operation (inverse Ackermann)
payload.concept: Path compression plus union by size make union-find nearly O(1) per operation
payload.example_bad: const find = x => (parent[x] === x ? x : find(parent[x])); // no compression, recursive
payload.explanation: Without optimisations, unions can build a chain, and find walks the whole chain: O(n) per call. Union by size attaches the smaller tree under the larger, which keeps trees shallow. Path compression makes every node visited by find point to the root (or, with halving, to its grandparent), so later finds take one step. Together they give an amortised cost bounded by the inverse Ackermann function, which is at most 4 for any realistic input. Write find iteratively, because a recursive find on a long chain throws RangeError before it gets the chance to compress anything.
payload.misconception: Union-find is fast with or without its optimisations.

metadata.concept: Use a Map as the parent table for labels, adding each label the first time it appears

payload.complexity: Nearly O(1) amortised per operation, plus hashing
payload.concept: Use a Map as the parent table for labels, adding each label the first time it appears
payload.explanation: When elements are strings such as emails or variable names, store parent links in a Map and add each element as its own parent the first time it appears. A plain {} already holds inherited keys, so a label such as 'constructor' looks present before it is added and its parent is a function. === compares strings by value, so roots compare correctly, unlike Java's ==. For many operations, map each label to an integer id once and use the array-based class, which is faster.
payload.misconception: A plain object works as the parent table for string labels.

metadata.concept: Store each node's ratio to its parent, and combine ratios along the path

payload.concept: Store each node's ratio to its parent, and combine ratios along the path
payload.example_bad:
weight.set(x, weight.get(x) * weight.get(p)); // before find(p): p's weight is not yet relative to the root
parent.set(x, find(p));
payload.explanation: Weighted union-find keeps weight(x) = value(x) / value(parent(x)). During find, after the parent has been compressed, multiply x's weight by its parent's weight, so x points straight at the root with the correct ratio. To union a / b = ratio, link a's root under b's root with weight ratio * weight(b) / weight(a). Two variables with the same root answer a / b as weight(a) / weight(b); different roots mean the answer is unknown.
payload.misconception: Ratio questions such as a / c from a / b and b / c need a graph search per query.

JavaScript · JavaScript Union-Find (Disjoint Set) · Core operations track
Union-find is two operations on one array. `find` walks to the root; `union` links two roots. Two optimisations keep the trees shallow: path compression (during `find`, point visited nodes closer to the root) and union by size (attach the smaller tree under the larger).

[Diagram: path compression · 4 elements, one group]

A chain like the one on the left forms when unions keep attaching the larger tree under the smaller; union by size prevents it, and path compression repairs it on the first `find`.

metadata.concept: Two pointers from both ends find a pair in a sorted array in O(n)

payload.complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space on sorted input
payload.concept: Two pointers from both ends find a pair in a sorted array in O(n)
payload.explanation: When the array is sorted, put one pointer at each end and look at the sum. If it is too small, only moving the left pointer right can increase it; if it is too large, only moving the right pointer left can decrease it. Each step discards one element for good, so the scan is O(n) time and O(1) space. The trick depends on sorted order; on unsorted input sort a copy first (and keep original indexes if the answer needs them) or use a Map.
payload.misconception: Finding two numbers that add up to a target needs a nested loop, or a sort followed by a search for each element.

metadata.concept: Skip equal neighbours after sorting so two-pointer searches return each combination once

payload.complexity: O(n^2) time, O(1) extra besides the sorted copy
payload.concept: Skip equal neighbours after sorting so two-pointer searches return each combination once
payload.explanation: Sort with a numeric comparator first (the default sort compares strings, so [10, 9, 1] would not be ordered). Fix the first element with an outer loop, run opposite pointers on the rest, and after every hit or move step past values equal to the one just used. Skip a repeated outer value too. Duplicates are never produced, so no set is needed, and the work stays O(n squared).
payload.misconception: A set of stringified triples is the natural way to remove duplicate results from 3Sum.

metadata.concept: A fixed-size window updates its total by adding the entering element and removing the leaving one

payload.concept: A fixed-size window updates its total by adding the entering element and removing the leaving one
payload.explanation: Adjacent windows share k-1 elements. Compute the first window once, then slide: add a[i] and subtract a[i - k]. Each element enters and leaves once, so the whole pass is O(n). Guard k > length first; a loop that assumes at least k elements returns -Infinity or a wrong value on short arrays.
payload.misconception: Each window of size k must be summed from scratch, which is O(n*k).

metadata.concept: A variable window grows on the right and shrinks from the left until its rule holds again

payload.concept: A variable window grows on the right and shrinks from the left until its rule holds again
payload.explanation: Expand the right edge one element at a time and record it. While the window is invalid, advance the left edge and undo its effect. Both edges only move forward, so the loop is O(n) even though it contains a while. Store the last-seen index in a Map to jump the left edge directly, but never move it backwards: use Math.max(left, last + 1). This works when removing an element can only make an invalid window better, as with non-negative numbers or distinct-character rules; with negative numbers use prefix sums instead.
payload.misconception: When a window breaks the rule, restart the scan from the next index.

metadata.concept: A prefix-sum array of length n+1 answers any range sum as a difference

payload.concept: A prefix-sum array of length n+1 answers any range sum as a difference
payload.explanation: Make prefix one longer than the input with prefix[0] = 0, so prefix[i] is the sum of the first i elements. The sum of a[l..r] inclusive is then prefix[r + 1] - prefix[l]. The extra leading zero removes the special case for ranges that start at index 0. Building is O(n) and each query is O(1), which pays off from the second query. It needs the data to stay fixed; for updates use a Fenwick or segment tree.
payload.misconception: prefix[i] is the sum of a[0..i], so a range sum is prefix[r] - prefix[l].

metadata.concept: Count subarrays with a target sum by storing how often each prefix sum has occurred

payload.concept: Count subarrays with a target sum by storing how often each prefix sum has occurred
payload.explanation: A subarray ending here sums to k when an earlier prefix equals current - k. Keep a Map from prefix sum to count, seeded with {0: 1} so subarrays that start at index 0 are counted, and add the count before inserting the current prefix. Windows fail with negatives because adding an element can lower the sum, so shrinking is no longer monotonic. Keys are numbers, so 0 and -0 are the same Map key (SameValueZero) and no special handling is needed.
payload.misconception: A sliding window counts subarrays that sum to k, even when the array has negative numbers.

metadata.concept: Binary search needs an integer midpoint, and JavaScript will not truncate it for you

payload.concept: Binary search needs an integer midpoint, and JavaScript will not truncate it for you
payload.explanation: JavaScript numbers are doubles, so (lo + hi) / 2 is 2.5 for lo = 2, hi = 3, and a[2.5] is undefined. Floor it with Math.floor. Doubles do not overflow here, but the bit shift is a trap: >> converts to a 32-bit integer first, so (2 ** 31) >> 1 is -1073741824. That breaks a search over answer values above 2^31 - 1, so prefer Math.floor. The lo + (hi - lo) form also carries over to Java. Pick one loop invariant (closed range lo <= hi, or half-open lo < hi) and keep it consistent in every branch.
payload.misconception: (lo + hi) / 2 is the middle index, as in a typed language where integer division truncates.

metadata.concept: A lower-bound search returns the first index that satisfies a monotone condition

payload.concept: A lower-bound search returns the first index that satisfies a monotone condition
payload.explanation: Searching for a boundary is more general than searching for a value. Use a half-open range [lo, hi) with hi = length, and while lo < hi test a condition that flips once from false to true. If mid fails the condition, lo = mid + 1; otherwise hi = mid. When the loop ends, lo is the first index that satisfies it, or length if none does. Lower bound is first index with a[i] >= x; upper bound is first index with a[i] > x; the number of occurrences is the difference.
payload.misconception: Binary search should return as soon as it finds the target, which is enough for first and last occurrences too.

metadata.concept: Binary search can run over answer values when feasibility is monotone

payload.complexity: O(n log max) time, O(1) space
payload.concept: Binary search can run over answer values when feasibility is monotone
payload.explanation: If you can test "is answer x enough?" in O(n), and larger x never makes a feasible answer infeasible, the answers are sorted by feasibility even though there is no array. Search the smallest feasible x between a lower and an upper bound: the largest element for a minimum speed, the sum for a minimum capacity. Use Math.ceil for divisions that must round up. Total cost is O(n log range), and each probe is a simple check function.
payload.misconception: Binary search only applies to sorted arrays.

metadata.concept: Two pointers from both ends find a pair in a sorted array in O(n)

payload.complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space on sorted input
payload.concept: Two pointers from both ends find a pair in a sorted array in O(n)
payload.explanation: On a sorted array, put one index at each end and look at the sum. Too small means only moving the left index right can help; too large means only moving the right index left can help. Each step discards one element, so the scan is O(n) time and O(1) space. Declare the sum as long when the values can be large, because int addition wraps silently and a wrapped negative sum sends a pointer the wrong way. On unsorted input, sort a copy with Arrays.sort or use a HashMap.
payload.misconception: Finding two numbers that add up to a target needs a nested loop.

metadata.concept: Skip equal neighbours after sorting so two-pointer searches return each combination once

payload.complexity: O(n^2) time, O(1) extra besides the sorted copy
payload.concept: Skip equal neighbours after sorting so two-pointer searches return each combination once
payload.explanation: Sort a copy, fix the first element with an outer loop, run opposite pointers on the rest, and after each hit step past values equal to the ones just used. Skip a repeated outer value as well. No duplicate triple is ever built, so no set is needed and the work stays O(n squared). Compute sums as long when inputs can approach the int limits, since a wrapped sum looks like a valid small one. Arrays.sort on int[] is a dual-pivot quicksort and needs no comparator.
payload.misconception: A HashSet of lists is the natural way to remove duplicate results from 3Sum.

metadata.concept: A fixed-size window updates its total by adding the entering element and removing the leaving one

payload.concept: A fixed-size window updates its total by adding the entering element and removing the leaving one
payload.explanation: Adjacent windows share k-1 elements. Sum the first window once, then slide: add a[i] and subtract a[i - k]. Each element enters and leaves once, so the pass is O(n). Keep the running total in a long when k times the largest value can pass about 2.1 billion; an int total wraps without any error. Guard k against the array length first, because a[i - k] throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException on short input.
payload.misconception: Each window of size k must be summed from scratch, and an int total is large enough.

metadata.concept: A variable window grows on the right and shrinks from the left until its rule holds again

payload.concept: A variable window grows on the right and shrinks from the left until its rule holds again
payload.explanation: Expand the right edge one element at a time. While the window is invalid, advance the left edge and undo its effect. Both edges only move forward, so the loop is O(n) even though it contains a while. For characters, an int[128] (or int[256]) of last-seen positions is faster than a HashMap<Character, Integer> and avoids boxing; jump the left edge with Math.max(left, last[c] + 1) so it never moves back. Use this only when removing an element can only help, as with distinct-character rules or non-negative numbers; with negative numbers use prefix sums.
payload.misconception: When a window breaks the rule, restart the scan from the next index.

metadata.concept: A prefix-sum array of length n+1 answers any range sum as a difference

payload.concept: A prefix-sum array of length n+1 answers any range sum as a difference
payload.explanation: Make prefix one longer than the input with prefix[0] = 0, so prefix[i] is the sum of the first i elements. The sum of a[l..r] inclusive is prefix[r + 1] - prefix[l]. The leading zero removes the special case for ranges that start at 0. Use long[] for the prefix: ten thousand values of 300,000 already exceed Integer.MAX_VALUE, and int overflow gives wrong answers with no exception. Building is O(n) and each query is O(1).
payload.misconception: A prefix array of ints is enough, and prefix[i] is the sum of a[0..i].

metadata.concept: Count subarrays with a target sum by storing how often each prefix sum has occurred

payload.concept: Count subarrays with a target sum by storing how often each prefix sum has occurred
payload.explanation: A subarray ending here sums to k when an earlier prefix equals current - k. Keep a HashMap<Long, Integer> from prefix to count, seeded with 0 -> 1, and read the count before inserting the current prefix. Use long keys so a large prefix is not silently wrapped, and getOrDefault to avoid null unboxing. Windows fail with negatives because adding an element can lower the sum, so shrinking is not monotonic.
payload.misconception: A sliding window counts subarrays that sum to k, even with negative numbers.

metadata.concept: The midpoint (lo + hi) / 2 can overflow int, so write lo + (hi - lo) / 2

payload.concept: The midpoint (lo + hi) / 2 can overflow int, so write lo + (hi - lo) / 2
payload.example_bad: int mid = (lo + hi) / 2; // negative when lo + hi passes Integer.MAX_VALUE
payload.explanation: Java int addition wraps at 2^31 - 1. With lo and hi both above a billion, lo + hi becomes negative and the index is invalid. This bug lived in the JDK's own binary search for years. Use lo + (hi - lo) / 2 or (lo + hi) >>> 1; the unsigned shift treats the wrapped sum as a 32-bit positive number. The same applies when binary searching an int answer range such as 1 to 2 billion, even though array sizes are smaller. Pick one loop invariant and keep it in every branch.
payload.misconception: (lo + hi) / 2 is always safe because both values are valid array indexes.

metadata.concept: A lower-bound search returns the first index that satisfies a monotone condition

payload.concept: A lower-bound search returns the first index that satisfies a monotone condition
payload.example_bad:
int i = Arrays.binarySearch(new int[]{1, 2, 2, 2, 5}, 2); // some index of a 2, not necessarily 1
int j = Arrays.binarySearch(new int[]{1, 3}, 2);            // -2, not -1
payload.explanation: Arrays.binarySearch returns any matching index when there are duplicates, and for a missing key returns -(insertionPoint) - 1, so the result for a miss is negative but not always -1. Write your own boundary search with a half-open range [lo, hi), hi = length. If a[mid] < x then lo = mid + 1, else hi = mid; at the end lo is the first index with a[i] >= x, or length if none. Upper bound uses a[mid] <= x. Occurrences are upper minus lower.
payload.misconception: Arrays.binarySearch returns the first matching index, or -1 when the key is absent.

metadata.concept: Binary search can run over answer values when feasibility is monotone

payload.complexity: O(n log max) time, O(1) space
payload.concept: Binary search can run over answer values when feasibility is monotone
payload.example_bad: hours += (int) Math.ceil(p / mid); // p / mid is already truncated
payload.explanation: If "is answer x enough?" is an O(n) check and larger x never turns a feasible answer infeasible, binary search the smallest feasible x between a lower and an upper bound. In Java, p / k on ints truncates before Math.ceil can see it, so use (p + k - 1) / k, or Math.ceilDiv from Java 18 on (this curriculum targets 17, so use the manual form). Accumulate the check's total in a long. Cost is O(n log range).
payload.misconception: Binary search only applies to sorted arrays, and Math.ceil(p / k) rounds up integer division.

metadata.concept: Array.prototype.sort reorders the original array and returns the same array

payload.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) for the copy
payload.concept: Array.prototype.sort reorders the original array and returns the same array
payload.explanation: sort works in place and returns a reference to the same array, so const sorted = a.sort() makes two names for one mutated array. Copy first with [...a].sort(cmp) or a.slice().sort(cmp), or use toSorted(cmp) on Node 20 and later. The sort has been stable since ES2019, so equal elements keep their original order, which matters for multi-key sorts. Sorting costs O(n log n) time; the copy adds O(n) space.
payload.misconception: sort returns a new sorted array and leaves the original alone.

metadata.concept: A comparator must return a number for every pair, and NaN counts as equal

payload.concept: A comparator must return a number for every pair, and NaN counts as equal
payload.example_bad:
const rows = [{ n: 3 }, {}, { n: 1 }, { n: 2 }];
rows.sort((a, b) => a.n - b.n); // unchanged: NaN counts as equal
payload.explanation: If a.n or b.n is undefined, the subtraction is NaN, and the sort treats NaN as zero, meaning "equal". An inconsistent comparator leaves the array in an implementation-defined order, with no error. Decide what missing values mean and handle them explicitly, for example by sorting them last. Do not return booleans either: a > b gives 1 or 0 and never a negative number. Compare with the three-way form when subtraction may not be valid, such as strings or mixed types.
payload.misconception: (a, b) => a.n - b.n sorts any objects by n.

JavaScript · sorting · ordering · L1
Concept: Sort by several keys with one comparator that falls through on ties
Misconception: Sorting by the second key and then again by the first key needs two passes and an unstable result.
Explanation: Because the sort is stable, two passes (secondary key first, then primary key) do work, but a single comparator is clearer: return the first non-zero comparison and fall through on ties. Strings compare with < and >, or localeCompare when language-aware ordering matters (localeCompare is slower, so avoid it in hot loops). Keep each key's direction explicit by swapping its operands.
Incorrect:
people.sort((a, b) => a.age - b.age);
people.sort((a, b) => a.name.localeCompare(b.name)); // second pass wins; ages are only a tie-break by accident
Correct:
const people = [{ name: 'Bo', age: 30 }, { name: 'Al', age: 30 }, { name: 'Cy', age: 25 }];
people.sort((a, b) => b.age - a.age || a.name.localeCompare(b.name)); // age desc, name asc
Complexity: O(n log n) comparisons

metadata.concept: Counting and bucket sort beat O(n log n) when keys are small integers or frequencies

payload.concept: Counting and bucket sort beat O(n log n) when keys are small integers or frequencies
payload.explanation: Frequencies are bounded by n, so bucket by count: build a Map of counts, then an array of n + 1 lists where index c holds the values that occurred c times, and read from the high end. Time is O(n). The same idea sorts small non-negative integers directly: count each value, then emit them in order. It does not apply when the key range is huge compared with n. Use new Array(n + 1).fill().map(() => []), because fill([]) would share one list.
payload.misconception: Top-k frequent elements needs a sort, or a heap, at O(n log n).

metadata.concept: Three-way partition sorts values 0, 1 and 2 in one pass with three pointers

payload.concept: Three-way partition sorts values 0, 1 and 2 in one pass with three pointers
payload.example_bad: if (a[mid] === 2) { [a[mid], a[high]] = [a[high], a[mid]]; high--; mid++; } // skips the swapped-in value
payload.explanation: Keep low (next slot for 0), mid (current), high (next slot for 2). If a[mid] is 0, swap with low and advance both; if 1, advance mid; if 2, swap with high and shrink high but do not advance mid, because the element that arrived from high has not been examined. One pass, O(n) time, O(1) space. The same partition handles less-than, equal-to and greater-than a pivot, which is how quicksort copes with many duplicates.
payload.misconception: After swapping with the high pointer, advance the middle pointer like any other swap.

metadata.concept: Merge sort counts inversions during the merge step

payload.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
payload.concept: Merge sort counts inversions during the merge step
payload.explanation: Split the array, sort both halves recursively, then merge. When the next element comes from the right half while i elements of the left half remain, each of those remaining left elements is greater than it, so add the number of remaining left elements to the count. Total time is O(n log n) and merge sort is stable. Use strict comparison on ties: taking the left element when equal (<=) keeps stability and avoids counting equal pairs. Allocate the merge buffer once for large inputs; recursion depth is only log n.
payload.misconception: Counting pairs that are out of order needs a nested loop at O(n squared).

metadata.concept: Quickselect finds the k-th element in average O(n) by partitioning one side only

payload.complexity: O(n) average, O(n^2) worst, O(n) space for the copy
payload.concept: Quickselect finds the k-th element in average O(n) by partitioning one side only
payload.example_bad: const kthLargest = (a, k) => [...a].sort((x, y) => y - x)[k - 1]; // O(n log n)
payload.explanation: Partition around a pivot; the pivot lands at its final index p. If p equals the target index, done; otherwise recurse (loop) into only the side that contains it. Average cost is O(n); a bad pivot on sorted input makes it O(n squared), so pick the pivot at random. Quickselect rearranges the array, so copy it if the caller needs the original. A heap of size k is O(n log k) and the right choice for streaming data or when the array must not be mutated.
payload.misconception: Finding the k-th largest requires sorting, or a heap of size k.

metadata.concept: In a rotated sorted array one half is always sorted, so decide which half holds the target

payload.complexity: O(log n) time for distinct values, O(1) space
payload.concept: In a rotated sorted array one half is always sorted, so decide which half holds the target
payload.example_bad: const find = (a, x) => a.indexOf(x); // O(n)
payload.explanation: At any mid, at least one of [lo, mid] and [mid, hi] is sorted. Compare a[lo] with a[mid] to find the sorted half, check whether the target lies inside that half's range, and discard the other half. This needs distinct values: with duplicates a[lo] === a[mid] tells you nothing and the worst case degrades to O(n). Use <= when comparing a[lo] with a[mid], because lo and mid can be the same index.
payload.misconception: Binary search cannot work once a sorted array has been rotated.

metadata.concept: Start at a corner of a row- and column-sorted matrix to discard a row or column each step

payload.concept: Start at a corner of a row- and column-sorted matrix to discard a row or column each step
payload.example_bad: const has = (m, t) => m.some(row => row.includes(t)); // O(m*n)
payload.explanation: When rows and columns both ascend, the top-right cell is the largest in its row and the smallest in its column. If it is greater than the target, drop its column; if smaller, drop its row. Each step removes a whole line, so the walk takes at most rows + cols steps, O(m + n). If each row also starts above the previous row's last element, the matrix is one sorted sequence and a single binary search over index / cols and index % cols gives O(log(m*n)). Check for an empty matrix and empty rows before reading matrix[0].length.
payload.misconception: Searching a sorted matrix needs a binary search per row.

metadata.concept: Arrays.sort and List.sort reorder the original and return nothing

payload.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) for the copy
payload.concept: Arrays.sort and List.sort reorder the original and return nothing
payload.explanation: Arrays.sort(int[]) returns void and sorts the array you pass, so it will not compile as an expression and it destroys the original order. Clone first with a.clone() or Arrays.copyOf(a, a.length). Primitive arrays use a dual-pivot quicksort (not stable, which is invisible for primitives); object arrays and lists use TimSort, which is stable. There is no comparator overload for int[]: to sort descending, sort ascending and reverse, or box into Integer[].
payload.misconception: Arrays.sort(a) returns a sorted copy, so int[] sorted = Arrays.sort(a) works.

metadata.concept: Compare with Integer.compare, never subtraction, because subtraction overflows

payload.concept: Compare with Integer.compare, never subtraction, because subtraction overflows
payload.example_bad:
Integer[] a = {1, Integer.MIN_VALUE};
Arrays.sort(a, (p, q) -> p - q); // [1, -2147483648]: not sorted
payload.explanation: The difference of two ints can exceed the int range and wrap. 1 - Integer.MIN_VALUE wraps to a negative number, so the comparator claims that 1 is smaller than Integer.MIN_VALUE, and the array comes out in the wrong order with no exception. Integer.compare(a, b) and Comparator.naturalOrder() are safe. The same holds for Long, where (int) (a - b) also truncates. Comparators that are inconsistent can make TimSort throw "Comparison method violates its general contract!" on larger inputs.
payload.misconception: (a, b) -> a - b is a correct ascending comparator for integers.

metadata.concept: Chain comparators with comparingInt and thenComparing for multi-key sorts

payload.concept: Chain comparators with comparingInt and thenComparing for multi-key sorts
payload.example_bad: people.sort((a, b) -> b.age() - a.age()); // overflow-prone and ignores the name tie-break
payload.explanation: Build the comparator from key extractors: comparingInt(Person::age).reversed().thenComparing(Person::name) sorts age descending, then name ascending. With an implicit lambda, comparing(p -> p.age()).reversed() fails to compile because the lambda parameter is inferred as Object; use a method reference, an explicit type, or Comparator.comparingInt. List.sort and Arrays.sort on objects are stable (TimSort), so ties keep their input order. Use comparingInt to avoid boxing.
payload.misconception: Comparator.comparing(p -> p.age()).reversed() reverses the age order, like the method-reference form.

metadata.concept: Counting and bucket sort beat O(n log n) when keys are small integers or frequencies

payload.concept: Counting and bucket sort beat O(n log n) when keys are small integers or frequencies
payload.explanation: Frequencies are bounded by n, so bucket by count: build a HashMap of counts, then a List<List<Integer>> with n + 1 lists where index c holds the values seen c times, and read from the high end. Time is O(n). Creating a generic array such as new List<Integer>[n + 1] does not compile; use a list of lists. For small non-negative int keys, an int[] of counts is both the fastest map and the sorted order. It does not apply when the key range is huge compared with n.
payload.misconception: Top-k frequent elements needs a sort or a priority queue, and List<Integer>[] is a fine bucket array.

metadata.concept: Three-way partition sorts values 0, 1 and 2 in one pass with three indexes

payload.concept: Three-way partition sorts values 0, 1 and 2 in one pass with three indexes
payload.example_bad: if (a[mid] == 2) { swap(a, mid, high); high--; mid++; } // skips the swapped-in value
payload.explanation: Keep low (next slot for 0), mid (current) and high (next slot for 2). If a[mid] is 0, swap with low and advance both; if 1, advance mid; if 2, swap with high and shrink high, but do not advance mid, because the value that arrived from high has not been examined. One pass, O(n) time, O(1) space. Java has no destructuring swap, so use a small helper or a temporary variable. The same partition handles less-than, equal and greater-than a pivot.
payload.misconception: After swapping with the high index, advance the middle index like any other swap.

metadata.concept: Merge sort counts inversions during the merge step, and the count needs a long

payload.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
payload.concept: Merge sort counts inversions during the merge step, and the count needs a long
payload.explanation: An array of n elements has up to n(n-1)/2 inversions. For n = 70,000 in reverse order that is 2,449,965,000, above Integer.MAX_VALUE, so an int counter wraps silently. Count in a long. When the next element comes from the right half while i elements of the left half remain, add (mid - i) to the count. Take the left element on ties (<=) to keep the sort stable and to ignore equal pairs. Use one auxiliary array allocated once, not a new array per merge.
payload.misconception: The number of inversions fits in an int because the array length does.

metadata.concept: Quickselect finds the k-th element in average O(n) by partitioning one side only

payload.complexity: O(n) average, O(n^2) worst, O(n) space for the clone
payload.concept: Quickselect finds the k-th element in average O(n) by partitioning one side only
payload.explanation: Partition around a pivot; the pivot lands at its final index p. If p equals the target index, done; otherwise loop into only the side that contains it. Average cost is O(n); with a fixed pivot, sorted input degrades to O(n squared), so pick the pivot at random (ThreadLocalRandom). Quickselect reorders the array, so clone it if the caller still needs the original. A PriorityQueue of size k is O(n log k) and suits streams or arrays that must not be touched.
payload.misconception: Finding the k-th largest requires sorting, or a heap of size k.

metadata.concept: In a rotated sorted array one half is always sorted, so decide which half holds the target

payload.complexity: O(log n) time for distinct values, O(1) space
payload.concept: In a rotated sorted array one half is always sorted, so decide which half holds the target
payload.example_bad: int i = Arrays.binarySearch(new int[]{4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2}, 0); // undefined result: input is not sorted
payload.explanation: Arrays.binarySearch assumes the whole array is sorted and returns garbage on a rotated one. At any mid, at least one of [lo, mid] and [mid, hi] is sorted. Compare a[lo] with a[mid] to find the sorted half, check whether the target lies in that half's range, and discard the other half. This needs distinct values: with duplicates, a[lo] == a[mid] tells you nothing and the worst case becomes O(n). Use <= for a[lo] versus a[mid], because lo and mid can be the same index.
payload.misconception: Binary search cannot work once a sorted array has been rotated, and Arrays.binarySearch still applies.

metadata.concept: Start at a corner of a row- and column-sorted matrix to discard a row or column each step

payload.concept: Start at a corner of a row- and column-sorted matrix to discard a row or column each step
payload.example_bad: for (int[] row : m) if (Arrays.binarySearch(row, t) >= 0) return true; // O(m log n), ignores column order
payload.explanation: When rows and columns both ascend, the top-right cell is the largest in its row and the smallest in its column. If it is greater than the target, drop its column; if smaller, drop its row. Each step removes a whole line, so the walk takes at most rows + cols steps, O(m + n). If each row also starts above the previous row's last element, one binary search over index / cols and index % cols gives O(log(m*n)). Check m.length == 0 and m[0].length == 0 before reading m[0], or the code throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
payload.misconception: Searching a sorted matrix needs a binary search per row.
