metadata.concept: Every recursion needs a base case, and JavaScript's call stack allows only about ten thousand frames

payload.complexity: O(n) time; recursion uses O(n) stack, the loop uses O(1)
payload.concept: Every recursion needs a base case, and JavaScript's call stack allows only about ten thousand frames
payload.example_bad:
const depth = (n) => (n === 0 ? 0 : 1 + depth(n - 1));
depth(100000); // RangeError
payload.explanation: Each call adds a stack frame, and V8 throws RangeError (Maximum call stack size exceeded) at roughly ten thousand frames, depending on frame size. Tail calls are not optimised in practice. A recursion that is correct for 1,000 items can crash at 100,000. Write the base case first, make sure each call moves toward it, and when depth can grow with the input, switch to a loop or an explicit stack. Recursion over a balanced tree is safe because depth is log n; over a list or a degenerate tree it is not.
payload.misconception: Recursion depth is only limited by memory, so a recursive function over a list of 100,000 items is fine.

metadata.concept: Memoise overlapping subproblems in a Map, and use BigInt once values pass 2^53

payload.concept: Memoise overlapping subproblems in a Map, and use BigInt once values pass 2^53
payload.explanation: Plain recursion recomputes the same subproblems, which makes fib exponential. Cache each result by its arguments and the cost drops to O(n). A Map handles any key you can build; for several arguments join them into a string such as `${i},${j}`. Numbers are doubles, exact only up to 2^53 - 1: fib(80) is 23416728348467685 but the Number version prints ...684. Use BigInt for exact large results, and keep the values in the Map as BigInt too, since BigInt and Number cannot be mixed in arithmetic.
payload.misconception: Fibonacci with a cache is exact for any n, because JavaScript numbers are big enough.

metadata.concept: Backtracking pushes a choice, recurses, pops it, and copies the path when recording

payload.concept: Backtracking pushes a choice, recurses, pops it, and copies the path when recording
payload.explanation: The path array is one object that every call mutates. Pushing path itself stores a reference, so after the search finishes every recorded entry is the same, empty, array. Record a copy ([...path]) at the moment you reach a result. The pattern is choose, explore, undo: for each element either skip it or push it, recurse, then pop. Subsets of n items number 2^n, so the cost is O(n * 2^n) because of the copies.
payload.misconception: out.push(path) records the current path.

metadata.concept: Skip a duplicate value unless its equal left neighbour is already in use

payload.concept: Skip a duplicate value unless its equal left neighbour is already in use
payload.explanation: Sort the input and keep a used flag per position. At each depth, skip index i when it is used, and skip it when a[i] equals a[i - 1] and a[i - 1] is not currently used: that means the equal twin was already tried at this position. This prunes duplicate branches instead of generating and discarding them. Without sorting, equal values are not adjacent and the rule fails. The count is n! divided by the product of the factorials of the repeat counts.
payload.misconception: Permutations of an array with repeated values need a Set of stringified results to remove duplicates.

metadata.concept: A start index prevents reordered duplicates, and sorting lets you stop a loop early

payload.complexity: Exponential in target / smallest candidate; pruning cuts most branches
payload.concept: A start index prevents reordered duplicates, and sorting lets you stop a loop early
payload.explanation: If every step loops from index 0, [2, 3] and [3, 2] are both produced. Pass a start index and loop from it, so a combination is built in index order. To allow reuse of the same number, recurse with i, not i + 1. Sort the candidates and break (not continue) as soon as one exceeds the remaining target, since every later candidate is larger. Copy the path when the remainder is 0.
payload.misconception: Combination sum can loop over all candidates at every step.

metadata.concept: Define the state first, then keep only the last values the recurrence reads

payload.concept: Define the state first, then keep only the last values the recurrence reads
payload.explanation: A DP needs a state meaning, a recurrence and a base. For house robber, best(i) is the most you can take from the first i houses, and best(i) = max(best(i-1), best(i-2) + a[i]). Because the recurrence reads only two earlier values, two variables replace the array and space drops to O(1). Choosing all even or all odd positions fails on [2, 1, 1, 2], where the best is 4 (first and last) and each parity gives 3. Write the recurrence before the code.
payload.misconception: Pick the larger of the even-index sum and odd-index sum to solve house robber.

metadata.concept: Fill an unreachable DP cell with Infinity, then translate it to -1 at the end

payload.concept: Fill an unreachable DP cell with Infinity, then translate it to -1 at the end
payload.explanation: dp[a] is the fewest coins that make amount a, with dp[0] = 0. Unreachable amounts need a value that never wins a min: Infinity works in JavaScript because Infinity + 1 is still Infinity. Using 0 as the filler makes unreachable cells look like the best answer. After the loops, return -1 if dp[amount] is still Infinity. Iterate amounts in the outer loop and coins in the inner loop to count minimum coins with reuse allowed.

payload.concept: In a 1D 0/1 knapsack the capacity loop runs downward so each item is used once
payload.example_bad:
for (let i = 0; i < w.length; i++)
  for (let c = w[i]; c <= cap; c++) dp[c] = Math.max(dp[c], dp[c - w[i]] + v[i]); // item reused
payload.explanation: dp[w] is the best value with capacity w. For each item, update dp[w] = max(dp[w], dp[w - weight] + value). If w runs upward, dp[w - weight] already includes the current item, so the item is used repeatedly: that is the unbounded knapsack. payload.concept: Build a two-dimensional DP table with independent rows and a zero border
payload.example_bad: const dp = new Array(a.length + 1).fill(new Array(b.length + 1).fill(0)); // one shared row
payload.explanation: fill with an array puts the same array object in every row, so writing dp[1][1] changes dp[i][1] for every i. Create each row separately with Array.from. For longest common subsequence, dp[i][j] is the length for the first i characters of a and the first j of b; the extra row and column of zeros are the empty-prefix base case, so there are no index -1 reads. payload.concept: Longest increasing subsequence drops from O(n squared) to O(n log n) with a tails array and lower bound
payload.explanation: tails[k] is the smallest possible last value of an increasing subsequence of length k + 1. For each x, find the first index whose tail is >= x (lower bound) and overwrite it, or append when x is larger than every tail. The length of tails is the answer, but the array itself is generally not a valid subsequence. Use lower bound for a strictly increasing result; use upper bound if equal values may repeat in a non-decreasing subsequence.

metadata.concept: Deep recursion throws StackOverflowError, which catch (Exception e) does not catch

payload.complexity: O(n) time; recursion uses O(n) stack, the loop uses O(1)
payload.concept: Deep recursion throws StackOverflowError, which catch (Exception e) does not catch
payload.example_bad:
static int depth(int n) { return n == 0 ? 0 : 1 + depth(n - 1); }
// depth(1_000_000) throws StackOverflowError; catch (Exception e) does not catch it
payload.explanation: The default thread stack allows roughly ten to twenty thousand frames for a simple method. Past that the JVM throws StackOverflowError, which is an Error and not an Exception, so catch (Exception e) lets it through. Do not rely on catching it; make the recursion shallow enough, or switch to a loop or an explicit Deque when depth can grow with the input. Write the base case first and make each call move toward it. Recursion over a balanced tree is safe because depth is log n; over a list or a degenerate tree it is not.
payload.misconception: A try/catch (Exception e) around a deep recursion will handle the failure.

metadata.concept: Do not call computeIfAbsent recursively, and watch where long overflows

payload.concept: Do not call computeIfAbsent recursively, and watch where long overflows
payload.explanation: HashMap.computeIfAbsent must not modify the map from inside its mapping function, and the recursive call does. Since Java 9 this throws ConcurrentModificationException. Check with containsKey or get, compute, then put. The result type matters as much as the cache: Fibonacci fits a long only up to fib(92) = 7540113804746346429; fib(93) wraps to a negative number with no error. Guard the input, or use BigInteger for larger n. For several arguments, use a long[][] filled with -1, or a record key.
payload.misconception: map.computeIfAbsent(n, k -> fib(k - 1) + fib(k - 2)) is a neat memoised Fibonacci.

metadata.concept: Backtracking adds a choice, recurses, removes it by index, and copies the path when recording

payload.concept: Backtracking adds a choice, recurses, removes it by index, and copies the path when recording
payload.explanation: The path list is one object that every call mutates. Adding path itself stores a reference, so after the search every recorded entry is the same, empty, list. Record a copy with new ArrayList<>(path). Undo with path.remove(path.size() - 1): on a List<Integer>, remove(int) removes by index, but remove(Object) removes the first equal value, so passing an Integer variable removes the wrong element. The pattern is choose, explore, undo. Subsets of n items number 2^n, so the cost is O(n * 2^n).
payload.misconception: out.add(path) records the current path, and path.remove(x) undoes the last add.

metadata.concept: Skip a duplicate value unless its equal left neighbour is already in use

payload.concept: Skip a duplicate value unless its equal left neighbour is already in use
payload.explanation: Sort the input and keep a boolean used per position. At each depth, skip index i when it is used, and skip it when a[i] equals a[i - 1] and a[i - 1] is not currently used: its equal twin was already tried at this position. This prunes duplicate branches instead of generating and discarding them. Without sorting, equal values are not adjacent and the rule fails. The count is n! divided by the product of factorials of the repeat counts.
payload.misconception: Permutations of an array with repeated values need a Set of lists to remove duplicates.

metadata.concept: A start index prevents reordered duplicates, and sorting lets you stop a loop early

payload.complexity: Exponential in target / smallest candidate; pruning cuts most branches
payload.concept: A start index prevents reordered duplicates, and sorting lets you stop a loop early
payload.explanation: If every step loops from index 0, [2, 3] and [3, 2] are both produced. Pass a start index and loop from it, so a combination is built in index order. To allow reuse of the same number, recurse with i, not i + 1. Sort the candidates and break (not continue) as soon as one exceeds the remaining target, since every later one is larger. Copy the path when the remainder is 0. Use int remainders; targets near Integer.MAX_VALUE are not realistic here.
payload.misconception: Combination sum can loop over all candidates at every step.

metadata.concept: Define the state first, then keep only the last values the recurrence reads

payload.concept: Define the state first, then keep only the last values the recurrence reads
payload.explanation: A DP needs a state meaning, a recurrence and a base. For house robber, best(i) is the most you can take from the first i houses, and best(i) = max(best(i-1), best(i-2) + a[i]). The recurrence reads only two earlier values, so two variables replace the array and space drops to O(1). All even or all odd positions fails on [2, 1, 1, 2], where the best is 4 and each parity gives 3. Use long totals when values or length can push the sum past 2.1 billion.
payload.misconception: Pick the larger of the even-index sum and odd-index sum to solve house robber.

metadata.concept: Use amount + 1 as the unreachable sentinel, because Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 wraps negative

payload.concept: Use amount + 1 as the unreachable sentinel, because Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 wraps negative
payload.explanation: dp[a] is the fewest coins that make amount a. Unreachable cells need a value that never wins a min. Java has no Infinity for int, and Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 wraps to Integer.MIN_VALUE, which then wins every min. Any real answer is at most amount (all 1-coins), so amount + 1 is a safe sentinel that cannot overflow. After the loops return -1 when dp[amount] is still amount + 1. Loop amounts outside and coins inside.
payload.misconception: Integer.MAX_VALUE is a safe "infinity" for a minimum, as Infinity is in JavaScript.

metadata.concept: In a 1D 0/1 knapsack the capacity loop runs downward so each item is used once

for (int i = 0; i < w.length; i++)
  for (int c = w[i]; c <= cap; c++) dp[c] = Math.max(dp[c], dp[c - w[i]] + v[i]); // item reused
payload.explanation: dp[w] is the best value with capacity w. For each item, update dp[w] = max(dp[w], dp[w - weight] + value). If w runs upward, dp[w - weight] already includes the current item, so the item is used repeatedly: that is the unbounded knapsack. For 0/1, loop w from capacity down to weight, so every read sees values from before this item. The direction of the inner loop is the whole difference between the two problems.

metadata.concept: Allocate a two-dimensional DP table with new int[m + 1][n + 1], never Arrays.fill with one row

payload.complexity: O(m * n) time and space; O(min(m, n)) space with rolling rows
payload.concept: Allocate a two-dimensional DP table with new int[m + 1][n + 1], never Arrays.fill with one row
payload.example_bad:
int[][] dp = new int[a.length() + 1][];
Arrays.fill(dp, new int[b.length() + 1]); // one shared row
payload.explanation: Arrays.fill puts the same int[] object in every slot, so writing dp[1][1] changes dp[i][1] for every i. new int[m + 1][n + 1] allocates separate rows, already zeroed. For longest common subsequence, dp[i][j] is the length for the first i characters of a and the first j of b; the extra row and column of zeros are the empty-prefix base case, so there are no index -1 reads. If characters match take dp[i-1][j-1] + 1, otherwise the larger of dp[i-1][j] and dp[i][j-1]. Compare chars with ==, not Strings.
payload.misconception: Arrays.fill(dp, new int[n + 1]) creates a table of zero rows I can fill independently.

metadata.concept: Longest increasing subsequence in O(n log n) with a tails array and Arrays.binarySearch

payload.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
payload.concept: Longest increasing subsequence in O(n log n) with a tails array and Arrays.binarySearch
payload.example_bad:
int i = Arrays.binarySearch(tails, x); // searches the unused zeros too, and a miss is negative
tails[i] = x;                          // ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException for negative i
payload.explanation: tails[k] is the smallest possible last value of an increasing subsequence of length k + 1. For each x, binary search the used part of tails. A found index means an equal tail exists, so overwriting it changes nothing, which is right for a strictly increasing result. A negative result is -(insertionPoint) - 1; convert it back with -(r + 1) and write x there, growing the size when the point equals it. The length is the answer, but tails itself is generally not a valid subsequence. Pass the size as the range end, because unused slots hold zeros.
payload.misconception: The tails array is the longest increasing subsequence, and a negative binarySearch result means not found.

payload.explanation: Greedy picks the locally best option and never reconsiders. That is correct only when an exchange argument shows the local choice can always be extended to an optimum. For coins 1, 5, 10, 25 it works. For coins 1, 3, 4 and amount 6, greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1 (three coins) but 3 + 3 uses two. When you cannot prove the greedy rule, test it against a brute force or DP on small inputs, or use DP. Interval scheduling by earliest end time and the jump game farthest-reach rule are greedy rules that do have proofs.

metadata.concept: Sort intervals by start with a numeric comparator, then extend the last merged interval with Math.max

payload.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
payload.concept: Sort intervals by start with a numeric comparator, then extend the last merged interval with Math.max
payload.explanation: With no comparator, sort converts each inner array to a string, so [10, 12] sorts before [2, 3]. Compare starts numerically. After sorting, an interval overlaps the last merged one when its start is at most that interval's end; use <= if touching intervals such as [1, 2] and [2, 3] should merge. Extend with Math.max(last end, end), because a later interval can sit entirely inside the earlier one, as [2, 3] does inside [1, 10]. Push copies so the input arrays are not mutated.
payload.misconception: intervals.sort() orders pairs by their first number, and the end of a merged interval is the later interval's end.

metadata.concept: To keep the most non-overlapping intervals, sort by end time and take each interval that starts after the last end

payload.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
payload.concept: To keep the most non-overlapping intervals, sort by end time and take each interval that starts after the last end
payload.example_bad: const a = [...iv].sort((x, y) => x[0] - y[0]); // by start: takes [1,10] first
payload.explanation: Finishing early leaves the most room for what follows, so sort by end and take an interval whenever its start is at or after the end of the last one taken (>= lets touching intervals coexist). Sorting by start fails: [1, 10] starts first and blocks [2, 3] and [4, 5], giving 1 instead of 2. The exchange argument: swapping any chosen interval for the one that ends earliest never makes the rest infeasible. The minimum removals to make the set non-overlapping is n minus this count.
payload.misconception: Sorting by start time and taking each interval that fits maximises the count.

metadata.concept: Insert into a sorted interval list in one pass with three phases

payload.concept: Insert into a sorted interval list in one pass with three phases
payload.example_bad: const out = merge([...intervals, newInterval]); // re-sorts a list that was already sorted
payload.explanation: The list is already sorted and disjoint, so one pass is enough. Phase one copies intervals that end before the new one starts. Phase two absorbs every interval whose start is at most the new end, growing the new interval with min and max. Phase three copies the rest. This is O(n) rather than O(n log n) and keeps the original order of the untouched intervals. Check the empty list and insertion at either end.
payload.misconception: Insert by appending the new interval, re-sorting and merging.

metadata.concept: Sort starts and ends separately to count the most meetings overlapping at once

payload.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
payload.concept: Sort starts and ends separately to count the most meetings overlapping at once
payload.example_bad:
const starts = iv.map(x => x[0]).sort();   // string order: 1, 20, 8
const ends = iv.map(x => x[1]).sort();
payload.explanation: The room count at any time is the number of meetings that started but not ended. Sort all starts and all ends independently. Walk the starts: if the next start is at or after the earliest unfinished end, a room frees up and is reused (advance the end pointer); otherwise a new room is needed. The final room count is the peak overlap. Use a numeric comparator: the default sort orders [1, 8, 20] as 1, 20, 8 and reports two rooms for three separated meetings. Using >= means a meeting that starts when another ends shares its room.
payload.misconception: Sorting starts and ends with the default sort is fine, because they are numbers.

metadata.concept: Track the farthest reachable index instead of choosing which jump to take

payload.concept: Track the farthest reachable index instead of choosing which jump to take
payload.explanation: Choosing where to land is the wrong question. Walk the array keeping far, the farthest index reachable from any index visited so far. If the current index exceeds far, you are stuck. Otherwise update far with i + a[i]. For [2, 3, 0, 1, 4], jumping to the farthest landing spot (index 2, a zero) strands you, yet index 1 reaches the end. The reach rule is correct because any index up to far is reachable. One pass, O(1) space.
payload.misconception: Always jump to the farthest index you can see from here.

metadata.concept: BFS gives shortest paths in an unweighted graph if you set the distance when a node is queued

payload.concept: BFS gives shortest paths in an unweighted graph if you set the distance when a node is queued
payload.explanation: BFS visits nodes in order of distance, so the first time a node is reached is its shortest distance. Record the distance and mark the node when you push it, not when you pop it; otherwise the same node can be queued once per incoming edge. Initialise distances to -1, so that -1 means unvisited, and stop when the target is dequeued. Array.shift is O(n) on large arrays, so move a head index through the array instead. BFS is wrong for weighted edges; use Dijkstra there.
payload.misconception: Mark a node visited when you take it off the queue, and queue.shift() is a fine dequeue.

metadata.concept: A graph is bipartite if two-colouring succeeds from every component

payload.concept: A graph is bipartite if two-colouring succeeds from every component
payload.explanation: Colour a start node 0, then give every neighbour the opposite colour; if a neighbour already has the same colour as the current node, an odd cycle exists and the answer is false. A graph can be disconnected, and an odd cycle can hide in a component that node 0 never reaches, so loop over every node and start a new BFS from each uncoloured one. Use -1 for uncoloured so that colour 0 is not mistaken for missing. Self-loops are never bipartite.
payload.misconception: Colouring from node 0 is enough to decide whether the whole graph is bipartite.
